People Who Never Reached Age 84

Victor Hugo

Birth date: February 25, 1802

Death date: May 21, 1885

Age: 83

Victor Hugo was a towering French Romantic author, poet, playwright, political figure, and campaigner for social causes, best known internationally for Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame. A national literary hero, he died in Paris on 22 May 1885 at age 83, commonly reported after pneumonia, and his death triggered extraordinary public mourning and a state funeral at the Panthéon.

Voltaire

Birth date: November 20, 1694

Death date: May 29, 1778

Age: 83

Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was one of the sharpest voices of the French Enlightenment: a playwright, historian, polemicist, philosopher and tireless critic of intolerance, censorship and religious dogmatism. His wit, especially in works such as Candide, made him a European celebrity and a lasting symbol of intellectual freedom. In 1778 he returned triumphantly to Paris after decades away, but his health deteriorated soon afterward. He died there on 30 May 1778, aged 83; because of his conflict with the Church, his burial initially became a sensitive and politically charged matter.

Sigmund Freud

Birth date: May 5, 1856

Death date: September 22, 1939

Age: 83

Sigmund Freud was an Austrian neurologist and the founder of psychoanalysis, whose ideas about the unconscious, repression, dreams, sexuality, and the structure of the mind reshaped psychology, literature, medicine, and modern culture. After fleeing Nazi-controlled Vienna for London in 1938, he spent his final months in Hampstead. He died on 23 September 1939 at age 83 after years of painful oral and jaw cancer; his physician Max Schur administered morphine at Freud’s request to relieve terminal suffering.

Albert Einstein

Birth date: March 13, 1879

Death date: April 17, 1955

Age: 76

Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist whose ideas reshaped modern science, especially through special and general relativity, mass-energy equivalence, and major contributions to quantum theory. Awarded the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, he became one of the most recognizable scientific figures of the twentieth century. He died in Princeton, New Jersey, at age 76 after internal bleeding from a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm; he declined further surgery and was said to have continued working close to the end.

Plato

Birth date: December 31, 429 BCE

Death date: December 31, 349 BCE

Age: 80

Plato was an Athenian philosopher, student of Socrates, teacher of Aristotle, and founder of the Academy, one of the most influential schools in the history of Western thought. Through dialogues such as the Republic, Symposium, Phaedo, and Timaeus, he shaped debates about justice, knowledge, politics, love, and the theory of Forms. He spent his final years back in Athens, teaching and writing; he died there around 348/347 BCE, probably in old age, with later tradition placing him at a wedding feast. His estimated age at death is 80.

Leo Tolstoy

Birth date: September 8, 1828

Death date: November 19, 1910

Age: 82

Leo Tolstoy was a Russian novelist, aristocrat, and moral thinker whose works, especially War and Peace and Anna Karenina, reshaped world literature with their psychological depth and sweeping realism. Late in life he became famous for his religious, pacifist, and social ideas. He died at age 82 of pneumonia at Astapovo railway station after leaving home during a dramatic final journey.

Confucius

Birth date: December 31, 551 BCE

Death date: December 31, 479 BCE

Age: 72

Confucius, born Kong Qiu, was the Chinese philosopher and teacher whose ideas on moral conduct, education, ritual, family duty, and virtuous government became the foundation of Confucianism and deeply shaped East Asian civilization. After years of political frustration, travel, and teaching, he returned to Lu, spent his final years instructing disciples and preserving classical traditions, and died around 479 BCE, probably from natural causes after personal losses and old age.

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was a German poet, novelist, playwright, scientist, statesman, and one of the defining figures of German literature, best known for works such as Faust and The Sorrows of Young Werther. His long career shaped Weimar Classicism and influenced European culture far beyond literature. He died in Weimar on 22 March 1832, aged 82, after a final period of declining health; accounts commonly describe his death as due to apparent heart failure.

Mahatma Gandhi

Birth date: October 1, 1869

Death date: January 29, 1948

Age: 78

Mahatma Gandhi, born Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, was an Indian lawyer, anti-colonial nationalist, and political ethicist whose philosophy of nonviolent resistance helped lead India’s struggle for independence from British rule and inspired civil rights movements worldwide. Revered by many as a moral and political leader, he spent his final months trying to calm communal violence after Partition. On 1948-01-30, at age 78, he was assassinated in New Delhi while on his way to an evening prayer meeting.

Death date: May 1, 1519

Age: 67

Leonardo da Vinci was the Italian Renaissance polymath whose paintings, anatomical studies, engineering designs, and notebooks made him one of history’s most influential artists and thinkers. Best known for the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, he spent his final years in France under royal patronage. He died at Clos Lucé near Amboise on 2 May 1519, aged 67, possibly after a stroke.

Karl Marx

Birth date: May 4, 1818

Death date: March 13, 1883

Age: 64
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Karl Marx is highly polarizing because his writings shaped revolutionary socialist and communist movements worldwide. Many readers associate Marxism with later one-party states, political repression, forced collectivization, and mass violence, even though Marx himself was a 19th-century theorist rather than a ruler.

Karl Marx was a German philosopher, economist, journalist, and revolutionary socialist whose analysis of capitalism and class conflict became one of the most influential bodies of political thought in modern history. With Friedrich Engels, he co-authored The Communist Manifesto, and his Das Kapital shaped later socialist, communist, and critical economic traditions. In his final years in London, Marx suffered declining health after the death of his wife Jenny; bronchitis and pleurisy followed a long period of illness, and he died there on 14 March 1883 at the age of 64.

Aristotle

Birth date: December 31, 384 BCE

Death date: December 31, 322 BCE

Age: 62

Aristotle was an ancient Greek philosopher and polymath from Stagira, a student of Plato and later tutor to Alexander the Great. His work shaped logic, biology, ethics, politics, metaphysics, rhetoric, and literary theory, and his Lyceum became the center of the Peripatetic school. After anti-Macedonian sentiment rose in Athens following Alexander’s death, Aristotle withdrew to Chalcis on Euboea, where he died in 322 BCE, traditionally associated with a longstanding stomach illness, at about 62.

Joseph Stalin

Birth date: December 17, 1878

Death date: March 4, 1953

Age: 74
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Joseph Stalin is one of the most controversial political leaders of the twentieth century. His rule involved dictatorship, forced collectivization, mass executions, purges, deportations, famine, censorship, labor camps, and extensive state terror, causing millions of deaths and long-lasting trauma across the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.

Joseph Stalin was a Georgian-born Soviet revolutionary and politician who ruled the Soviet Union for nearly three decades, serving as Communist Party general secretary and later premier. His rule transformed the USSR into a major industrial and military power, but it was also marked by dictatorship, forced collectivization, purges, mass repression, famine, and the expansion of Soviet influence after World War II. In his final years he grew increasingly suspicious and isolated. He suffered a stroke at his Kuntsevo dacha and died in Moscow on 5 March 1953 at the age of 74, triggering a tense succession struggle among Soviet leaders.

Galileo Galilei

Birth date: February 14, 1564

Death date: January 7, 1642

Age: 77

Galileo Galilei was an Italian astronomer, physicist, mathematician, and engineer whose telescopic observations transformed astronomy and strengthened the case for heliocentrism. He studied motion, improved scientific instruments, and became a central figure in the Scientific Revolution. After his trial by the Roman Inquisition, he spent his final years under house arrest near Florence, blind and in poor health, yet still working on ideas that shaped modern physics. He died in Arcetri on 8 January 1642 at the age of 77.

Age: 73

Charles Robert Darwin was an English naturalist whose work transformed biology by explaining evolution through natural selection. His 1859 book On the Origin of Species became one of the most influential scientific works ever published. Darwin died at Down House in Kent on 19 April 1882, aged 73, after long-standing health problems; he was later buried with national honors in Westminster Abbey.

Age: 79

Immanuel Kant was a Prussian-German philosopher from Königsberg and one of the defining figures of the Enlightenment. His Critique of Pure Reason, moral philosophy, and theory of knowledge reshaped modern thought and influenced ethics, metaphysics, aesthetics, and political theory. In his final years his health and mental powers declined; he died in Königsberg on 12 February 1804, aged 79, reportedly after saying, “It is good.”

Death date: April 29, 1945

Age: 56
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Extremely controversial because he was the Nazi dictator whose regime initiated the Second World War in Europe and carried out the Holocaust and other mass murders, persecutions, and aggressive wars.

Adolf Hitler was an Austrian-born German politician, leader of the Nazi Party, and dictator of Germany from 1933 to 1945. His regime launched the Second World War in Europe and was central to the Holocaust, the genocide of about six million Jews and millions of other victims. In April 1945, with Berlin surrounded by Soviet forces and Nazi Germany collapsing, Hitler withdrew into the Führerbunker and died by suicide on 30 April 1945, aged 56.

William Shakespeare was an English playwright, poet, and actor from Stratford-upon-Avon, celebrated as the leading dramatist of the English language. His plays, sonnets, and narrative poems shaped world literature and theatre for centuries. He died in Stratford on 23 April 1616, traditionally his 52nd birthday; the precise cause of death is not known, though he was buried two days later at Holy Trinity Church.

Socrates

Birth date: June 3, 469 BCE

Death date: June 14, 399 BCE

Age: 70

Socrates was an Athenian philosopher whose relentless questioning of ethics, virtue, knowledge, and civic life helped shape the foundations of Western philosophy. He wrote nothing himself, but his ideas survive through students such as Plato and Xenophon. In 399 BCE, after a tense political period in Athens, he was convicted of impiety and corrupting the young, refused escape, and died at about 70 by drinking poison hemlock.

Birth date: May 6, 1861

Death date: August 6, 1941

Age: 80

Rabindranath Tagore was a Bengali poet, writer, composer, painter, philosopher, and social reformer whose work reshaped modern Indian literature and music. He became the first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature in 1913, especially celebrated for Gitanjali, and his songs later became national anthems for India and Bangladesh. His final years were marked by chronic illness and severe episodes of decline; after a period of prolonged suffering, he died in the Jorasanko mansion in Calcutta, the house where he had been born.

Mao Zedong

Birth date: December 25, 1893

Death date: September 8, 1976

Age: 82
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Mao Zedong is one of the most controversial political figures of the twentieth century. His rule was tied to authoritarian repression, political purges, the Great Leap Forward famine, the Cultural Revolution, mass persecution, and policies associated with enormous human suffering and death.

Mao Zedong was a Chinese revolutionary, political theorist, and the founding leader of the People's Republic of China, ruling as the dominant figure of the Chinese Communist Party from 1949 until 1976. His era reshaped China through communist consolidation, mass campaigns, the Great Leap Forward, and the Cultural Revolution, leaving a vast and deeply contested legacy. In his final years his health deteriorated, and after a series of serious heart attacks he died in Beijing on 9 September 1976 at the age of 82.

Michael Jackson

Birth date: August 28, 1958

Death date: June 24, 2009

Age: 50
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Michael Jackson is highly controversial because of repeated allegations of child sexual abuse, major criminal and civil proceedings, and later documentary accounts that kept public debate active after his death. He was acquitted in his 2005 criminal trial and denied the allegations, so the controversy includes both serious accusations and disputed legal/public interpretations.

Michael Jackson was an American singer, songwriter, dancer, and global pop icon whose music, videos, choreography, and style reshaped popular entertainment. From his childhood with the Jackson 5 to solo milestones such as Off the Wall, Thriller, Bad, and Dangerous, he became one of the best-selling and most influential performers in history. He died in Los Angeles on June 25, 2009, at age 50, from cardiac arrest linked to acute propofol and sedative intoxication while preparing for his This Is It concert series.

Thomas Jefferson

Birth date: April 12, 1743

Death date: July 3, 1826

Age: 83
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Thomas Jefferson is highly controversial because he enslaved hundreds of people while publicly writing about liberty and equality. His relationship with Sally Hemings, an enslaved woman in his household, and his lifelong dependence on slavery are central moral contradictions in his legacy.

Thomas Jefferson was an American Founding Father, principal author of the Declaration of Independence, third president of the United States, advocate of religious liberty, architect of Monticello, founder of the University of Virginia, and a major but deeply contradictory figure because he enslaved hundreds of people. He died at Monticello on July 4, 1826, the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration, after declining health in his final months; he was 83.

Augustus

Birth date: September 22, 63 BCE

Death date: August 18, 14

Age: 75

Caesar Augustus, born Gaius Octavius and later known as Octavian, was the founder of the Roman Empire and its first emperor, ruling from 27 BC until AD 14. He turned the exhausted Roman Republic into the Principate, reshaped government, expanded imperial administration, and gave his name to an age of relative stability known as the Pax Romana. He died at Nola in southern Italy on 19 August AD 14, apparently from natural causes; rumors that Livia poisoned him persisted, but were never proven. He was succeeded by Tiberius and deified by the Senate.

George Washington was a Virginia planter, military commander, Founding Father, and the first president of the United States, serving from 1789 to 1797. He led the Continental Army to victory in the American Revolutionary War and helped establish many precedents for the presidency. He died at Mount Vernon on December 14, 1799, after a sudden severe throat illness, with later medical discussion often pointing to epiglottitis and the effects of aggressive bloodletting.

Muhammad

Birth date: April 21, 570

Death date: June 7, 632

Age: 62
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Muhammad is a deeply revered religious figure for Muslims and also a historically contested political and military leader. Discussion of his wars, marriages, succession, lawgiving, and any visual depiction of him can be highly sensitive, and his legacy is often drawn into modern religious and political conflict.

Muhammad was an Arab religious, political, and military leader from Mecca who founded Islam and proclaimed the revelations that became the Qur'an. He united much of Arabia through preaching, diplomacy, and conflict, and his teachings became central to one of the world's major religions. In 632, shortly after the Farewell Pilgrimage, he fell ill in Medina with fever and severe pain and died in the house of his wife Aisha, leaving a rapidly expanding Muslim community without a clearly uncontested succession.

Archimedes

Birth date: December 31, 287 BCE

Death date: December 31, 212 BCE

Age: 75

Archimedes of Syracuse was one of antiquity’s greatest mathematicians, physicists, engineers, astronomers, and inventors. His work on geometry, mechanics, hydrostatics, levers, and the famous Archimedes’ principle made him a foundational figure in scientific history. He also designed defensive machines during the Roman siege of Syracuse. When the city fell, he was killed by a Roman soldier during the sack, despite later traditions saying the Roman commander had wanted him spared.

Age: 83

Otto von Bismarck was the Prussian statesman who engineered German unification and became the first chancellor of the German Empire, ruling through Realpolitik, diplomacy, and a hard-edged political style that earned him the nickname the Iron Chancellor. After being forced from office in 1890, he spent his final years in Friedrichsruh writing memoirs and criticizing Kaiser Wilhelm II. His health declined badly in the 1890s, with reports of foot gangrene, pain, fever, breathing trouble, and increasing dependence on a wheelchair. He died at Friedrichsruh on 1898-07-30 at the age of 83.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Lenin is highly controversial because he founded and led a one-party revolutionary state, used political repression against opponents, and is associated with the Red Terror, civil-war coercion, censorship, and the creation of institutions that shaped later Soviet authoritarianism.

Vladimir Lenin, born Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, was a Russian revolutionary, Marxist theorist, founder of the Bolshevik faction, and the first head of government of Soviet Russia and later the Soviet Union. He led the October Revolution of 1917 and shaped the one-party Soviet state through policies including nationalization, civil-war centralization, and the New Economic Policy. After a series of debilitating strokes in 1922 and 1923, Lenin’s health collapsed; he died at Gorki on 21 January 1924 at the age of 53.

Johann Sebastian Bach was a German composer, organist, and master of the late Baroque era, celebrated for works such as the Brandenburg Concertos, the St Matthew Passion, The Well-Tempered Clavier, and the Mass in B minor. His music combined intellectual architecture, expressive depth, and spiritual intensity in a way that shaped Western classical music for centuries. In his final years he suffered from severe eye problems; after unsuccessful eye surgery and a reported stroke, he died in Leipzig on 28 July 1750 at the age of 65.

Augustine of Hippo was a North African Christian theologian, philosopher, bishop, and one of the most influential writers in Western Christianity. Born in Thagaste, he became famous for works such as Confessions and The City of God, blending classical philosophy with Christian doctrine. He served as bishop of Hippo Regius for decades. In his final months, the Vandals besieged Hippo; already gravely ill, Augustine spent his last days in prayer and penitence and died there on 28 August 430 at age 75.

Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra was the Spanish writer whose Don Quixote reshaped European fiction and made him a defining figure of Spanish literature. A former soldier, captive in Algiers, playwright, poet, and novelist, he turned a turbulent life into a work of comic genius and deep human insight. In his final years in Madrid he remained financially strained but still productive, completing late works while ill. He died on 22 April 1616, probably after a painful illness often associated with symptoms of diabetes, and was buried the next day in the Convent of the Barefoot Trinitarians.

Why this is controversial: Julius Caesar is controversial as a conqueror and authoritarian political leader. His campaigns in Gaul caused mass death, enslavement, and displacement, and his crossing of the Rubicon, civil war, and dictatorship helped destroy the Roman Republic.

Julius Caesar was a Roman general, statesman and author whose conquest of Gaul, alliance with Pompey and Crassus, victory in civil war and dictatorship reshaped the Roman Republic and helped prepare the Roman Empire. After accepting the title dictator for life in 44 BC, he was stabbed to death by a senatorial conspiracy led by Brutus and Cassius on the Ides of March, an assassination that triggered another round of civil wars.

Why this is controversial: Henry Ford is highly controversial because he promoted virulent antisemitism through publications such as The International Jew, which influenced extremist and Nazi antisemitic propaganda. His labor practices, anti-union actions, and authoritarian control over workers also contribute to the controversy around his legacy.

Henry Ford was an American industrialist and the founder of the Ford Motor Company, best known for the Model T and for making automobile ownership possible for millions through high-volume production and the moving assembly line. His ideas reshaped manufacturing worldwide, though his legacy is also shadowed by his antisemitic publications. In his final years, after earlier strokes and declining health, Ford died at his Fair Lane estate in Dearborn, Michigan, on April 7, 1947, from a cerebral hemorrhage. He was 83.

He died in Bournemouth on 2 September 1973, aged 81, after suffering a bleeding ulcer and chest infection.

His growing deafness made his career even more extraordinary. After several months of serious illness marked by symptoms such as jaundice, swelling, and abdominal fluid, he died in Vienna on 26 March 1827 at the age of 56.

Napoleon Bonaparte, later Napoleon I, was a Corsican-born French general and statesman who rose during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French. He reshaped Europe through military campaigns, state reforms, and the Napoleonic Code, leaving a legacy admired for administrative modernization and criticized for war, authoritarian rule, and the restoration of slavery in French colonies. After his defeat at Waterloo, he was exiled to Saint Helena, where his health declined. He died at Longwood House on 5 May 1821, aged 51, most commonly attributed to stomach cancer.

He died in Ravenna in September 1321, aged 56, most likely from malaria contracted after returning from a diplomatic mission to Venice.

Richard Milhous Nixon was the 37th president of the United States, serving from 1969 until 1974, and remains the only U.S. president to resign from office. A Republican from California, he previously served as a congressman, senator, and vice president under Dwight D. Eisenhower. His presidency included major foreign-policy moves such as opening relations with China and pursuing détente with the Soviet Union, but it was overshadowed by the Watergate scandal. Nixon suffered a severe stroke at his home in New Jersey on April 18, 1994, slipped into a coma, and died four days later in New York at age 81.

In his final years he remained in Göttingen but suffered increasing illness, especially heart disease; he died there on 23 February 1855, aged 77, and was buried in the Albani Cemetery.

Best known for works such as The Social Contract, Émile, and Confessions, he blended philosophy with a strikingly personal literary style. Rousseau died suddenly at Ermenonville, France, on 2 July 1778, only four days after his 66th birthday; his death is generally attributed to cerebral bleeding or an apoplectic stroke.

In his final year his health declined from liver disease, commonly identified as cirrhosis; he died at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul on 10 November 1938, aged 57.

Sarah Bernhardt was a French stage actress, born Henriette-Rosine Bernard, and one of the first truly international theatre celebrities. She toured widely across Europe and the Americas and remained active after the amputation of her leg in 1915. In her final years her health declined from kidney disease and uremia; she collapsed again in March 1923 while still involved in film work at home, and died in Paris on 26 March 1923 at the age of 78.

Diagnosed with motor neuron disease as a young man, he lived far beyond early expectations and continued working for decades. He died peacefully at his home in Cambridge on 14 March 2018, aged 76, and his ashes were later interred in Westminster Abbey near Isaac Newton and Charles Darwin.

Through the Voyages extraordinaires, including Journey to the Center of the Earth, Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas, and Around the World in Eighty Days, he turned geography, engineering, and exploration into popular literary drama. In later life he lived in Amiens, remained publicly active, and endured worsening health. He died at home on 24 March 1905, aged 77, while suffering from chronic diabetes and complications from a stroke that had paralyzed his right side.

René Descartes was a French philosopher, mathematician, and scientist whose method of radical doubt and famous idea “I think, therefore I am” helped shape modern philosophy. He also linked algebra and geometry, giving his name to Cartesian coordinates. In 1649 he moved to Stockholm to tutor Queen Christina of Sweden; the cold climate, early-morning lessons, and illness are traditionally connected with the pneumonia that led to his death on 11 February 1650, at age 53.

He died in Hanover on 14 November 1716 at age 70; by then he had fallen from court favor, his funeral was sparsely attended, and his grave remained unmarked for decades.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Christopher Columbus is highly controversial because his voyages are tied to European colonization of the Americas, Indigenous dispossession, forced labor, enslavement, violence, and catastrophic population loss. He is also criticized for his conduct as governor in the Caribbean and for becoming a symbol in modern debates over conquest and colonial memory.

Christopher Columbus was a Genoese navigator and explorer whose four Spanish-sponsored Atlantic voyages transformed European knowledge of the Americas and helped launch a long era of exploration, conquest, and colonization. Ambitious, skilled, and controversial, he sought a westward route to Asia but reached Caribbean lands instead. After years of illness, disputes over titles and revenues, and declining royal favor, he died in Valladolid, Spain, on 20 May 1506, still convinced he had reached the fringes of Asia. He was 54.

Queen Victoria, born Alexandrina Victoria, ruled the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until 1901 and became Empress of India in 1876. Her 63-year reign defined the Victorian era, a period of industrial growth, imperial expansion, social change, and a reshaped constitutional monarchy. In her final weeks her health declined at Osborne House on the Isle of Wight, where she died on 22 January 1901 at the age of 81, with her son and successor Edward VII among those present.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Richard Wagner is highly controversial because of his explicit antisemitic writings, German nationalist politics, and the later embrace of his music and image by Adolf Hitler and Nazi cultural propaganda. His artistic importance is often discussed separately from these views, but the controversy is central to his public legacy.

Richard Wagner was a German composer, theatre director, conductor, and essayist whose operas transformed 19th-century music through their scale, mythology, leitmotifs, and idea of the Gesamtkunstwerk, or total work of art. His major works include The Ring of the Nibelung, Tristan und Isolde, Lohengrin, Tannhäuser, and Parsifal. In his final years he suffered worsening heart trouble, including severe angina attacks. After the 1882 Bayreuth Festival, he spent the winter in Venice, where he died of a heart attack at Ca’ Vendramin Calergi on 13 February 1883, aged 69.

A committed parliamentarian, secular humanist, and advocate of scientific modernization, he helped shape India’s democratic institutions and non-aligned foreign policy. His health declined in his final years; after returning to New Delhi from a short rest in Dehradun, he collapsed following pain in his back and died in office on 27 May 1964, with the cause widely described as a heart attack.

He died in Nishapur on 4 December 1131 at about 83; the precise cause is not securely recorded, though later accounts connect his final years with declining health and a quiet return to his hometown, where his tomb became famous for the story of blossoms falling over it.

After losing office, he wrote the works that made his name synonymous with hard-headed political realism. He died near Florence in 1527, aged 58, after suffering from a stomach illness; he received last rites and was later buried in the Basilica of Santa Croce.

Genghis Khan, born Temüjin, was the Mongol leader who united the steppe tribes and founded the Mongol Empire in 1206, creating one of history’s most formidable military powers. His campaigns reshaped Eurasia, reaching deep into China and Central Asia. He died in August 1227, aged about 65, during the final campaign against Western Xia; later accounts link his decline to illness, possibly after a fall from a horse, and his burial place remains unknown.

Kim Il Sung, born Kim Song Ju, was a North Korean revolutionary and politician who founded the Democratic People's Republic of Korea in 1948 and ruled it until his death. He built a highly centralized dictatorship, shaped the state ideology around his leadership, and became the first figure in the Kim family dynasty. Death date: August 11, 1955

Age: 80

Thomas Mann was one of the defining German-language novelists of the 20th century, celebrated for Buddenbrooks, Death in Venice, The Magic Mountain, and Doctor Faustus. Awarded the 1929 Nobel Prize in Literature, he combined irony, psychological depth, and social criticism, and became an outspoken opponent of Nazism in exile. He died in Zurich on 12 August 1955, shortly after his 80th birthday, following a final illness later identified as a perforated iliac artery aneurysm with internal bleeding complications.

Dmitri Ivanovich Mendeleev was a Russian chemist whose periodic law and periodic table turned a scattered list of elements into a predictive scientific system, helping chemistry become a more organized modern science. He also worked on petroleum, metrology, education, and industrial chemistry. In his final years he remained internationally honored but never received the Nobel Prize; he died in Saint Petersburg on 2 February 1907, aged 72, after an illness commonly described as influenza, sometimes linked with pneumonia.

Death date: September 10, 1971

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Nikita Khrushchev was a Soviet leader tied to an authoritarian one-party state, repression, censorship, Cold War confrontation, the crushing of the 1956 Hungarian uprising, and policies that caused serious social and political harm. He is also associated with de-Stalinization, but his rule remains highly controversial.

Nikita Khrushchev was the Soviet leader who followed Joseph Stalin, serving as First Secretary of the Communist Party and later as premier. He is remembered for de-Stalinization, the “Secret Speech,” the Cuban Missile Crisis, the space-race era, and his earthy, unpredictable political style. After being removed from power in 1964, he lived in forced retirement. Khrushchev died of a heart attack in Moscow’s Central Clinical Hospital on 11 September 1971, aged 77, and was buried at Novodevichy Cemetery rather than in the Kremlin Wall.

Death date: October 11, 1924

Age: 80

Anatole France, born François-Anatole Thibault, was a French novelist, poet, critic, journalist, member of the Académie française, and winner of the 1921 Nobel Prize in Literature. Admired for his elegant irony, skepticism, and humane style, he became one of the best-known French literary figures of his age, with works such as The Crime of Sylvestre Bonnard, Thaïs, Penguin Island, and The Gods Are Athirst. In later life he was also known for public engagement, including his support for Alfred Dreyfus and his pacifist views after World War I. He died on 12 October 1924 at Saint-Cyr-sur-Loire, near Tours, aged 80, after a period of failing health; France honored him with a national funeral.

Elizabeth I was Queen of England and Ireland from 1558 to 1603, the last Tudor monarch and a defining ruler of the Elizabethan era, remembered for religious compromise, political caution, maritime expansion, and the cultural world of Shakespeare and the Armada. She died at Richmond Palace after years of declining health. No post-mortem was permitted, so the precise cause is uncertain; suggested explanations include blood poisoning, pneumonia, cancer, or a severe throat infection such as quinsy.

His overthrow and death during the Libyan civil war remain politically charged.

Muammar Gaddafi was a Libyan military officer and revolutionary who seized power in a 1969 coup and ruled Libya for more than four decades, building an idiosyncratic authoritarian system shaped by Arab nationalism, anti-Western rhetoric, oil wealth, and his own political theories. In 2011, during the First Libyan Civil War, his regime collapsed after a NATO-backed uprising; he was captured near Sirte and killed by rebel forces on 20 October 2011.

Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Andrew Jackson is one of the most controversial U.S. presidents because he was a slave owner and because his administration pursued Indian removal policies that led to forced displacement and mass suffering, including the Trail of Tears. His military campaigns against Native peoples and forceful executive style add to the severity of the controversy around his legacy.

Andrew Jackson was the seventh president of the United States, a military commander, lawyer, congressman, senator, and the central figure of Jacksonian Democracy. Known as “Old Hickory,” he rose to national fame after the Battle of New Orleans and reshaped the presidency with a forceful populist style, while his legacy remains deeply controversial because of slavery and policies toward Native Americans. In his final years at the Hermitage near Nashville, his health deteriorated badly; he suffered from dropsy, tuberculosis, and heart failure before dying on June 8, 1845, at age 78.

Woodrow Wilson was the 28th president of the United States, a former Princeton University president and governor of New Jersey, and a central figure in World War I diplomacy and the League of Nations. His legacy combines major Progressive Era reforms and the Nobel Peace Prize with serious criticism of his racial policies. After a severe stroke in 1919 left him weakened and partly disabled, his health declined after leaving office, and he died at his Washington, D.C. home on February 3, 1924, aged 67.

Already weakened by illness, he collapsed after performing as Argan in The Imaginary Invalid and died in Paris a few hours later, aged 51.

He died around 232 BCE, probably after a long reign of about 36 to 37 years; Buddhist traditions remember his last days as marked by illness and final acts of religious generosity.

Benito Mussolini was an Italian politician, journalist, and dictator who founded Fascism and ruled Italy as Il Duce from 1922 until his overthrow in 1943. He turned Italy into a one-party dictatorship, aligned with Nazi Germany, and led the country into World War II. He led North Vietnam through years of war and political struggle, but died of heart failure at his home in Hanoi on 1969-09-02, while the Vietnam War was still unresolved; he was 79.

Boris Yeltsin was a Soviet and Russian politician who became the first president of the Russian Federation, serving from 1991 to 1999 during the turbulent transition after the collapse of the Soviet Union. He was known for confronting the 1991 coup attempt, pushing market reforms, and presiding over a dramatic reshaping of Russian politics. He died in Moscow on 23 April 2007 at age 76, with reports citing heart failure or congestive heart failure.

John Maynard Keynes was an English economist, mathematician by training, public intellectual, and one of the most influential economic thinkers of the twentieth century. His work reshaped modern macroeconomics, especially through Keynesian economics and the argument that governments could use spending, taxation, and monetary policy to fight recessions and mass unemployment. During and after the Second World War he also played a major role in designing the postwar financial order. Exhausted by public service and international negotiations, he suffered a series of heart attacks in 1946 and died at his home near Firle, Sussex, aged 62.

His rule was marked by authoritarian control, wars with Iran and Kuwait, and severe repression of opponents. Awarded the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac, he also became widely known for the Schrödinger’s cat thought experiment. After years in Austria, Germany, Britain, and Ireland, he returned to Vienna in later life. He died there on 1961-01-04 at age 73, after a long illness; tuberculosis is commonly cited as the cause of death.

Matsuo Bashō was the great Edo-period Japanese poet who transformed haikai and later became celebrated as the supreme master of haiku. Born near Ueno in Iga Province, he built a life around teaching, travel, literary experiment, and sharply observed scenes of nature and impermanence. Following the death of his wife, he moved to New York City to live with his daughter, where he died on July 4, 1831, at age 73, reportedly from heart failure and tuberculosis.

Yasser Arafat was a central Palestinian political leader, chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization, president of the Palestinian Authority, founder and leader of Fatah, and a 1994 Nobel Peace Prize co-laureate for the Oslo peace process. A symbol of Palestinian national aspirations and a deeply controversial figure internationally, he spent his final years under intense political pressure and confinement in Ramallah. Albert Camus

Birth date: November 6, 1913

Death date: January 3, 1960

Age: 46

Albert Camus was a French-Algerian writer, philosopher, journalist, playwright, and one of the defining literary voices of the twentieth century. Born in French Algeria, he became famous for works such as The Stranger, The Plague, The Myth of Sisyphus, The Fall, and The Rebel, and received the 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature. His writing explored absurdity, revolt, moral responsibility, and human dignity in a violent century. Camus died on 4 January 1960 at age 46 in a car crash near Sens, France, while traveling in a Facel Vega driven by his friend and publisher Michel Gallimard.

Johannes Kepler

Birth date: December 26, 1571

Death date: November 14, 1630

Age: 58

Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer, mathematician, astrologer, and natural philosopher whose laws of planetary motion transformed astronomy and helped lay the foundations of modern science. He worked with Tycho Brahe, served as imperial mathematician, and wrote influential works including Astronomia nova, Harmonice Mundi, and the Rudolphine Tables. In 1630 he traveled to Regensburg to pursue unpaid imperial salary claims, fell ill after arriving, and died there on 15 November at age 58.

Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky

Birth date: May 6, 1840

Death date: November 5, 1893

Age: 53

Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian Romantic-era composer whose vivid melodies and dramatic orchestration made works such as Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty, The Nutcracker, the 1812 Overture, Eugene Onegin, and the Pathétique Symphony central to the classical repertoire. He brought Russian music to an international audience while blending Western conservatory technique with a deeply personal expressive style. He died in Saint Petersburg on 6 November 1893, aged 53. His death is traditionally attributed to cholera and its complications, though later speculation about suicide has remained controversial and is not supported by firm documentary evidence.

Albrecht Dürer

Birth date: May 20, 1471

Death date: April 5, 1528

Age: 56

Albrecht Dürer was the defining artist of the German Renaissance: a painter, engraver, printmaker, and theorist whose woodcuts, engravings, portraits, and studies of proportion carried his reputation across Europe. He worked from Nuremberg, travelled to Italy and the Low Countries, and became admired by artists and patrons far beyond Germany. After returning from the Netherlands in 1521, he suffered years of failing health and produced less art while focusing on theoretical writings. He died in Nuremberg on 6 April 1528, aged 56, and was buried in the Johannisfriedhof cemetery.

Eleanor Roosevelt was an American political figure, diplomat, writer, and activist who transformed the role of First Lady during Franklin D. Roosevelt’s presidency and later became a leading voice for human rights at the United Nations, helping advance the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. She died in New York City on November 7, 1962, at age 78, after serious illness involving aplastic anemia, disseminated tuberculosis, and heart failure.

William Blake

Death date: August 11, 1827

Age: 69

William Blake was an English poet, painter, engraver, and printmaker whose visionary art and poems helped shape Romantic literature and visual culture. Best known for works such as Songs of Innocence and of Experience, The Tyger, The Lamb, and Jerusalem, he was often overlooked in his lifetime but later became one of Britain’s most distinctive creative figures. He died in London on 12 August 1827 at age 69, after a long final illness; later medical scholarship has suggested liver disease, possibly biliary cirrhosis with pulmonary complications, though the exact diagnosis remains uncertain.

Death date: June 17, 1928

Age: 55

Roald Amundsen was a Norwegian polar explorer and one of the defining figures of the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration. He led the first successful expedition through the Northwest Passage and, in 1911, became the first person to reach the South Pole. In June 1928, he disappeared in the Arctic while flying a rescue mission for the crashed Italia airship; wreckage was later found, but his body was never recovered.

André Gide

Birth date: November 21, 1869

Death date: February 18, 1951

Age: 81

André Gide was a French novelist, essayist, dramatist, moral thinker, and one of the most influential literary figures of modern France. Awarded the 1947 Nobel Prize in Literature, he wrote works such as The Immoralist, Strait Is the Gate, The Pastoral Symphony, and The Counterfeiters, often exploring sincerity, desire, faith, freedom, and moral conflict. His career stretched from Symbolism to anti-colonial and anti-Stalinist criticism. Gide died in Paris on 19 February 1951 at age 81; several biographical sources report pneumonia as the immediate cause, and he was later buried at Cuverville in Normandy.

Age: 69

Octave Mirbeau was a French novelist, playwright, journalist, pamphleteer, and art critic, remembered for fierce social satire, anticlerical writing, and works such as The Torture Garden, The Diary of a Chambermaid, and Business Is Business. A defender of avant-garde artists and a politically combative public voice, he remained hard to classify. In his final years his health declined, World War I deepened his bitterness and pacifist despair, and he died in Paris on 16 February 1917, his sixty-ninth birthday.

Death date: July 18, 1374

Age: 69

Petrarch, born Francesco Petrarca, was an Italian poet, scholar, and early humanist whose Latin learning and Italian lyric poetry helped shape Renaissance culture. His Canzoniere and his devotion to classical manuscripts made him one of the defining literary minds of the 14th century. He spent his final years in Arquà near Padua, still reading and writing despite age and illness, and died during the night of 18–19 July 1374, traditionally remembered as being found in his study with his head resting on his books.

Qin Shi Huang

Birth date: January 31, 259 BCE

Death date: July 11, 210 BCE

Age: 49
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Qin Shi Huang was an authoritarian imperial ruler whose legacy includes wars of conquest, harsh Legalist punishments, forced labor on enormous state projects, censorship, and traditional accounts of book burning and executions of scholars. Some details of those accounts are debated, but his rule is strongly associated with coercive centralized power.

Qin Shi Huang, born Ying Zheng, was the founder of the Qin dynasty and the first emperor of a unified China. After defeating the rival Warring States, he centralized rule, standardized writing, weights, measures and coinage, expanded roads and walls, and left behind the famous mausoleum guarded by the Terracotta Army. He died in 210 BC during his fifth inspection tour of eastern China after becoming seriously ill; later tradition links his final years to an obsession with immortality, and mercury-based elixirs have often been suggested as a possible factor, though the exact cause remains uncertain.

William Butler Yeats

Birth date: June 12, 1865

Death date: January 27, 1939

Age: 73

William Butler Yeats was an Irish poet, dramatist, critic, and one of the defining voices of modern literature. A central figure in the Irish Literary Revival and a co-founder of the Abbey Theatre, he received the 1923 Nobel Prize in Literature for poetry that gave powerful artistic expression to Ireland’s national spirit. In later life, despite declining health, he remained creatively active. He died of heart failure on 28 January 1939 at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, near Menton in France, aged 73; he was first buried privately in France, and his remains were later moved to Drumcliff, County Sligo.

He died at age 67 after being shot while giving a campaign speech in Nara during Japan’s 2022 upper-house election campaign.

Taylor died in Los Angeles on March 23, 2011, at age 79, after years of health problems and a final hospitalization for congestive heart failure.

Peter Paul Rubens was the dominant Flemish Baroque painter of the 17th century, celebrated for grand religious, mythological, allegorical, and portrait works full of movement, color, and dramatic energy. Pearl S. Buck was an American writer and humanitarian whose fiction helped introduce many Western readers to Chinese family life and rural society. Later in life she supported adoption, civil rights, and cross-cultural causes. She died of lung cancer in Danby, Vermont, on March 6, 1973, shortly before her 81st birthday, and was buried at Green Hills Farm in Pennsylvania.

Henri-Louis Bergson was a French philosopher whose ideas about time, memory, intuition, duration, and creative evolution made him one of the most influential thinkers of the early twentieth century. A professor at the Collège de France and winner of the 1927 Nobel Prize in Literature, he shaped debates across philosophy, psychology, literature, and modernism. In his last years, weakened by rheumatic illness and living in German-occupied Paris, he refused special exemption from anti-Jewish laws. He died in Paris on 1941-01-04, aged 81, after a final illness described by sources as bronchitis, pneumonia, or pulmonary congestion.

Pope John XXIII, born Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli, was an Italian Catholic leader who served as pope from 1958 to 1963 and became one of the most warmly remembered pontiffs of the modern era. Known as the “Good Pope,” he opened the Second Vatican Council and pushed the Church toward dialogue, pastoral renewal, and engagement with the modern world. In his final months he suffered from stomach cancer; after hemorrhages and a perforated stomach led to peritonitis, he died in Vatican City on 3 June 1963 at the age of 81.

Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and one of history’s best-known Stoic philosophers, remembered for the Meditations and for ruling during the later Pax Romana. He died aged 58 while on campaign in the Danubian region, probably at Vindobona or near Sirmium, of unknown causes; later tradition often associates the period with the Antonine Plague.

Virginia Woolf was an English novelist, essayist, publisher, and critic, widely regarded as one of the defining modernist writers of the 20th century. Hernán Cortés

Birth date: December 31, 1485

Death date: December 1, 1547

Age: 62
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Hernán Cortés is highly controversial because he was a central figure in the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire. His legacy is tied to colonial violence, warfare, coercion, forced labor, cultural destruction, and the broader catastrophe experienced by Indigenous peoples after European conquest.

Hernán Cortés was a Spanish conquistador, military commander, explorer, and later Marquis of the Valley of Oaxaca. Born in Medellín, Castile, around 1485, he went to the Caribbean before leading the 1519 expedition that, through warfare, diplomacy, Indigenous alliances, and the siege of Tenochtitlan, helped bring down the Aztec Empire and place much of central Mexico under Castilian rule. In later life he struggled with debt, court disputes, and fading political influence. While attempting to press his claims and hoping to return to Mexico, he became ill near Seville and died at Castilleja de la Cuesta on 2 December 1547, probably from dysentery and pleurisy.

Akbar the Great was the third Mughal emperor, ruling from 1556 to 1605 and transforming the Mughal state into one of the most powerful and culturally influential empires of early modern Asia. In early October 1605 he fell seriously ill, commonly described as dysentery, and died later that month at about 63; he was succeeded by his son Jahangir and buried at Sikandra near Agra.

James Buchanan

Birth date: April 22, 1791

Death date: May 31, 1868

Age: 77
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: James Buchanan is highly controversial because his presidency is widely associated with the failure to confront the secession crisis before the American Civil War. He supported or accommodated pro-slavery political positions and is often ranked among the least effective U.S. presidents.

James Buchanan Jr. was the 15th president of the United States, serving from 1857 to 1861 after a long career as a congressman, senator, diplomat, and secretary of state. A Pennsylvania Democrat, he is remembered for his failure to prevent the secession crisis that led to the Civil War. After leaving office, he retired to Wheatland near Lancaster, Pennsylvania, defended his presidency in writing, and died there on June 1, 1868, after a cold worsened into respiratory failure. He was 77.

Richard Phillips Feynman was an American theoretical physicist, celebrated for his work in quantum electrodynamics, his vivid teaching style, and the Feynman diagrams that changed how physicists visualize particle interactions. Jane Austen

Birth date: December 15, 1775

Death date: July 17, 1817

Age: 41

Jane Austen was an English novelist whose sharply observant fiction transformed the novel of manners and helped shape literary realism. Best known for Pride and Prejudice, Sense and Sensibility, Emma, Mansfield Park, Persuasion, and Northanger Abbey, she wrote with wit, irony, and unusual insight into class, marriage, money, and women’s limited choices in Georgian society. Her fame grew greatly after her death, and her books have remained central to English literature. In her final year she suffered a serious, poorly understood illness, moved to Winchester to seek medical help, and died there on 18 July 1817 at the age of 41; later theories have included Addison’s disease, Hodgkin lymphoma, lupus, tuberculosis, and cancer.

Stanley Kubrick

Birth date: July 25, 1928

Death date: March 6, 1999

Age: 70

Stanley Kubrick was an American filmmaker, screenwriter, producer, and photographer whose meticulous visual style and daring themes made him one of cinema’s most influential directors. His films, including Paths of Glory, Dr. Strangelove, 2001: A Space Odyssey, A Clockwork Orange, The Shining, Full Metal Jacket, and Eyes Wide Shut, reshaped modern filmmaking with their precision, ambiguity, and psychological force. Kubrick died unexpectedly on March 7, 1999, at Childwickbury Manor in Hertfordshire, England, after suffering a heart attack in his sleep, only days after showing a final cut of Eyes Wide Shut. He was 70.

Seneca

Birth date: December 31, 5 BCE

Death date: April 11, 65

Age: 68

Seneca the Younger was a Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist, statesman, and one of the most influential writers of the early Roman Empire. Born in Corduba and educated in Rome, he became tutor and later adviser to Emperor Nero, while producing enduring moral essays, letters, and tragedies. In 65 CE, after the Pisonian conspiracy against Nero, Seneca was ordered to die by suicide; he opened his veins, took poison unsuccessfully, and died after a prolonged, staged Stoic farewell.

Birth date: March 3, 1678

Death date: July 27, 1741

Age: 63

Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was a Venetian Baroque composer, virtuoso violinist, priest, and impresario whose concertos helped define the solo concerto form. Best known for The Four Seasons, he wrote hundreds of instrumental works, sacred music, and operas, many connected with the Ospedale della Pietà in Venice. Near the end of his life he moved to Vienna hoping for new patronage, but Emperor Charles VI died soon after. Vivaldi fell into poverty and died there in 1741, reportedly from an internal infection or inflammation, and was buried simply in a hospital cemetery.

Timur

Death date: February 17, 1405

Age: 68
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Timur is highly controversial because his empire was built through extremely violent conquest. Historical accounts associate his campaigns with massacres, mass enslavement, destruction of cities, and terror tactics across Central Asia, Persia, India, the Middle East, and Anatolia, even though he was also a major patron of architecture and culture.

Timur, better known in the West as Tamerlane, was a Turco-Mongol conqueror from Transoxiana and the founder of the Timurid Empire. From his base at Samarkand, he built a vast military power across Central Asia, Iran, Afghanistan, India, parts of Russia, Syria and Anatolia, combining ruthless conquest with major patronage of architecture, scholarship and the arts. He died at Otrar in February 1405 while preparing or advancing for a campaign toward China, after falling ill in winter; his body was taken back to Samarkand and buried in the Gur-e Amir.

Age: 62

Émile Zola was a French novelist, journalist, playwright, and the leading voice of literary naturalism, best known for the Rougon-Macquart cycle, Germinal, and his courageous role in the Dreyfus Affair through J'Accuse...!. His writing combined social observation with moral urgency, making him one of the most influential European authors of the 19th century. He died in Paris at 62 from carbon monoxide poisoning caused by a blocked or badly ventilated chimney, a death officially treated as accidental but long surrounded by suspicion because of his political enemies.

Epicurus was an ancient Greek philosopher born on Samos who founded Epicureanism, a school centered on modest pleasure, friendship, clear thinking, and freedom from fear. His Garden in Athens became one of the great philosophical communities of the Hellenistic world and admitted followers beyond the usual elite circles. He died in Athens in 270 BC after a painful urinary stone illness, reportedly remaining composed and faithful to his teachings until the end.

During his third voyage, a dispute at Kealakekua Bay in Hawaii escalated into violence, and Cook was killed there on 14 February 1779 at the age of 50.

Romain Rolland was a French novelist, dramatist, essayist, art historian, musicologist, and committed pacifist, best known for the novel cycle Jean-Christophe and for receiving the 1915 Nobel Prize in Literature. He died in Vézelay, France, on 30 December 1944, aged 78, near the end of a war-torn era he had spent much of his life resisting through words and conscience.

Peter the Great, born Peter I Alekseyevich Romanov, was Tsar of Russia and later the first Emperor of Russia. He is remembered for transforming Russia into a major European power through military reform, naval expansion, administrative restructuring, Westernizing cultural policies, and the founding of Saint Petersburg. His reign reshaped the Russian state and left institutions that endured long after him. In his final years he suffered serious urinary and bladder illness; he died in Saint Petersburg on 8 February 1725 at the age of 52, with later accounts describing complications including uremia and gangrene of the bladder.

Jalal al-Din Muhammad Rumi was a 13th-century Persian-language poet, Islamic scholar, theologian, and Sufi mystic whose Masnavi became one of the most influential works of mystical literature. His teachings on divine love, longing, and spiritual transformation shaped the Mevlevi tradition and reached far beyond the medieval Islamic world. In December 1273 he fell ill in Konya, where he died on 17 December at age 66. His funeral was reportedly mourned by Muslims, Christians, and Jews, and he was buried beside his father at the site later known as the Green Tomb.

His regime reshaped Spanish politics through repression, censorship, nationalism, and close control of public life. In his final years he suffered prolonged illness; the official account states that he died in Madrid on 20 November 1975, aged 82, after which Spain entered the transition toward democracy.

Max Weber was a German sociologist, historian, jurist, and political economist whose work helped shape modern sociology and social theory. He died there on 14 June 1920 at age 56, from pneumonia often linked to the influenza pandemic, leaving major work unfinished.

He prepared calmly for death, completed a short autobiography, and died at his Edinburgh home on 25 August 1776, aged 65.

Grover Cleveland

Birth date: March 17, 1837

Death date: June 23, 1908

Age: 71

Grover Cleveland was the 22nd and 24th president of the United States, remembered as the only president to serve two nonconsecutive terms before the modern era and as a reform-minded Democrat of the Gilded Age. A former mayor of Buffalo and governor of New York, he built his reputation on opposition to corruption, wasteful spending, and political favoritism. After leaving public office, his health declined over several years; he became seriously ill in 1907 and died of a heart attack at his Princeton, New Jersey, residence on June 24, 1908, at the age of 71.

Alan Turing

Birth date: June 22, 1912

Death date: June 6, 1954

Age: 41

Alan Mathison Turing was an English mathematician, logician, cryptanalyst and pioneering computer scientist whose work shaped theoretical computer science, artificial intelligence and modern computing. During the Second World War he played a crucial role at Bletchley Park in breaking German ciphers, including Enigma-related naval traffic. After the war he designed early stored-program computer concepts and explored mathematical biology. In 1952 he was prosecuted for homosexual acts and underwent hormone treatment instead of imprisonment. He died in Wilmslow, Cheshire, on 7 June 1954 from cyanide poisoning; the inquest ruled suicide, though later discussion has noted that accidental poisoning cannot be entirely excluded.

Erasmus

Birth date: October 27, 1469

Death date: July 11, 1536

Age: 66

Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam was a Dutch Renaissance humanist, Catholic priest, theologian, philologist, and one of the most influential scholars of early modern Europe. His editions of the New Testament and writings such as The Praise of Folly helped reshape biblical scholarship, education, and religious debate on the eve of the Reformation. In his final years he was frail and living again in Basel, where he died on 12 July 1536 after an attack of dysentery and was buried in Basel Minster.

Friedrich Schiller

Birth date: November 9, 1759

Death date: May 8, 1805

Age: 45

Friedrich Schiller was a major German playwright, poet, philosopher, and historian, central to Weimar Classicism and remembered for works such as The Robbers, Don Carlos, William Tell, and Ode to Joy. A close collaborator and friend of Goethe, he helped shape modern German literature and dramatic thought. Schiller’s final years were marked by serious chronic illness, especially lung disease often described as tuberculosis. He died in Weimar on 9 May 1805 at the age of 45, while still creatively active.

Raphael

Birth date: April 5, 1483

Death date: April 5, 1520

Age: 37

Raphael, born Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino, was one of the defining artists of the High Renaissance, celebrated for the clarity, harmony, and grace of works such as The School of Athens, his Madonnas, and the Vatican Rooms. Alongside Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo, he is remembered as part of the classic Renaissance triad. He died in Rome on April 6, 1520, at age 37, probably after a sudden fever or acute illness, while still at the height of his artistic powers.

Johannes Brahms

Birth date: May 6, 1833

Death date: April 2, 1897

Age: 63

Johannes Brahms was one of the central composers of the Romantic era, admired for combining emotional depth with classical discipline. Born in Hamburg, he became a brilliant pianist and a master of symphonies, chamber music, piano works, songs, and choral music, including A German Requiem. In his final year, his health declined after diagnoses involving jaundice and cancer, commonly reported as liver cancer; he made a last public appearance in March 1897 and died in Vienna on 3 April 1897 at the age of 63.

Ulysses S. Grant

Birth date: April 26, 1822

Death date: July 22, 1885

Age: 63

Ulysses S. Grant was the Union general whose campaigns helped bring the American Civil War to a decisive end, and he later served as the 18th president of the United States from 1869 to 1877. His presidency was closely tied to Reconstruction, civil rights enforcement, and the difficult work of rebuilding the postwar nation. In his final months, suffering from throat cancer and financial ruin, he worked intensely on his memoirs, completing them shortly before his death on July 23, 1885.

Lewis Carroll

Death date: January 13, 1898

Age: 65

Lewis Carroll, born Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, was an English author, mathematician, photographer, poet, and Anglican deacon whose playful logic and verbal invention shaped Victorian literature. He is best known for Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and Through the Looking-Glass, works that turned nonsense, riddles, and dreamlike fantasy into enduring classics. He died in Guildford on 1898-01-14 at age 65, after influenza led to pneumonia, just under two weeks before his 66th birthday.

Honoré de Balzac

Birth date: May 19, 1799

Death date: August 17, 1850

Age: 51

Honoré de Balzac was a French novelist, playwright, critic, and journalist, celebrated as one of the great founders of literary realism. His vast cycle La Comédie humaine mapped post-Napoleonic French society with extraordinary detail, ambition, and psychological depth. After years of punishing work habits, debts, and worsening health, he married Ewelina Hańska in March 1850. He died in Paris five months later, aged 51, with medical accounts associating his death with gangrene and congestive heart failure.

Horace

Birth date: December 7, 65 BCE

Death date: November 26, 8 BCE

Age: 56

Horace, born Quintus Horatius Flaccus, was one of ancient Rome’s great lyric poets, admired for the Odes, Satires, Epistles, and Ars Poetica. From modest origins in Venusia, he studied in Rome and Athens, fought on the losing republican side at Philippi, then rebuilt his life as a poet under the patronage of Maecenas in the age of Augustus. He died in Rome on 27 November 8 BC, reportedly after a sudden illness, only days before his 57th birthday, and was buried near Maecenas.

Death date: November 16, 1796

Age: 67

Catherine the Great was the German-born empress of Russia from 1762 to 1796, one of the most powerful rulers of the eighteenth century. She expanded Russian territory, promoted Enlightenment ideas, patronized the arts, and strengthened Russia’s role in European politics. In November 1796 she suffered a stroke, fell into a coma, and died the following evening at the age of 67.

Enrico Fermi

Birth date: September 28, 1901

Death date: November 27, 1954

Age: 53

Enrico Fermi was an Italian-American physicist whose rare command of both theory and experiment helped shape modern nuclear and particle physics. A Nobel Prize winner in 1938, he developed key ideas in Fermi-Dirac statistics, beta decay, and neutron physics, and led the team that achieved the first controlled self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction at Chicago Pile-1. After the war he continued teaching and researching at the University of Chicago. He died in Chicago on 28 November 1954 from stomach cancer, aged 53, after an illness that cut short one of the most influential scientific careers of the twentieth century.

Leonard Cohen

Birth date: September 20, 1934

Death date: November 6, 2016

Age: 82

Leonard Cohen was a Canadian songwriter, singer, poet, and novelist whose deep voice, literary precision, and spiritual melancholy made him one of the most distinctive artists of the late twentieth century. Known for songs such as "Suzanne", "Bird on the Wire", and "Hallelujah", he explored love, faith, desire, politics, aging, and mortality with rare elegance. He died in Los Angeles on 2016-11-07 at age 82, reportedly in his sleep after a fall at home; leukemia was also cited as a contributing cause.

Benjamin Disraeli

Birth date: December 20, 1804

Death date: April 18, 1881

Age: 76

Benjamin Disraeli, 1st Earl of Beaconsfield, was a British Conservative politician, novelist, and one of the defining figures of Victorian politics. He served twice as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, helped shape the modern Conservative Party, promoted imperial policy, and became famous for his rivalry with William Ewart Gladstone. In his final year, after losing office in 1880, his health declined sharply; long troubled by asthma and gout, he developed bronchitis and died at his home in Mayfair, London, on 19 April 1881, aged 76.

François Mitterrand

Birth date: October 25, 1916

Death date: January 7, 1996

Age: 79

François Mitterrand was a towering figure of modern French politics, serving as President of France from 1981 to 1995 and becoming the first Socialist president of the Fifth Republic. His long presidency shaped France’s left, European integration, and the country’s late-20th-century political identity. He died in Paris on 8 January 1996 at age 79 from prostate cancer, an illness that had been largely hidden from the public during his years in office.

Charles Baudelaire

Birth date: April 8, 1821

Death date: August 30, 1867

Age: 46

Charles Baudelaire was a French poet, essayist, translator, and art critic whose Les Fleurs du mal helped reshape modern poetry with its urban intensity, musical language, and unsettling beauty. A major influence on Symbolism and literary modernism, he also translated Edgar Allan Poe and wrote sharply about art and modern life. His final years were marked by debt, illness, and collapse: after a massive stroke in 1866, he suffered paralysis and aphasia, spent time in care in Brussels and Paris, and died in Paris on 31 August 1867 at the age of 46.

Death date: March 7, 1874

Age: 74

Millard Fillmore was the 13th president of the United States, serving from 1850 to 1853 after the death of Zachary Taylor. A Whig from New York, he rose from poverty to become a lawyer, congressman, vice president, and president, and is remembered for supporting the Compromise of 1850 and enforcing the Fugitive Slave Act. After leaving office, he remained active in civic life in Buffalo. He suffered a stroke in February 1874 and died in Buffalo on March 8, 1874, at the age of 74.

Golda Meir

Birth date: May 2, 1898

Death date: December 7, 1978

Age: 80
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Golda Meir is highly controversial because of her leadership during the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the Yom Kippur War. Critics focus on her policies toward Palestinians, her rejection of Palestinian national identity in public statements, settlement and security policies, and perceived failures before the 1973 war.

Golda Meir was a Kyiv-born Jewish stateswoman who became one of the central figures of Israel’s founding generation and served as Israel’s prime minister from 1969 to 1974, the country’s first and only female head of government. Known for her blunt political style and wartime leadership during the Yom Kippur War, she remained an influential public figure after leaving office. She died in Jerusalem on 8 December 1978 at age 80 after a long struggle with cancer, commonly described as lymphatic cancer or lymphoma, and was buried on Mount Herzl.

Calvin Coolidge

Birth date: July 3, 1872

Death date: January 4, 1933

Age: 60

Calvin Coolidge was the 30th president of the United States, serving from 1923 to 1929 after first rising through Massachusetts politics as a lawyer, governor, and vice president. Known as “Silent Cal,” he became associated with limited government, fiscal restraint, and the prosperity of the 1920s. After leaving office, he returned to Northampton, Massachusetts, wrote and spoke publicly, and lived a comparatively quiet retirement. He died suddenly at home on January 5, 1933, from coronary thrombosis, a form of heart-related clotting, at the age of 60.

Death date: April 26, 1972

Age: 62

Kwame Nkrumah was the central leader of Ghana’s independence movement, the first prime minister of independent Ghana and later its first president. A forceful Pan-Africanist and political theorist, he helped found the Organisation of African Unity and became one of the most recognizable anti-colonial figures of the 20th century. Overthrown in a 1966 coup while abroad, he lived his final years in exile in Guinea. He died in Bucharest, Romania, on 27 April 1972 while receiving treatment for prostate cancer, aged 62.

Age: 45

Freddie Mercury, born Farrokh Bulsara in Zanzibar, was the electrifying lead vocalist and pianist of Queen, celebrated for his four-octave voice, theatrical stagecraft, and classics such as “Bohemian Rhapsody,” “Somebody to Love,” and “We Are the Champions.” He helped turn Queen into one of rock’s most iconic bands, with his 1985 Live Aid performance remaining legendary. Diagnosed with AIDS in the late 1980s, he kept working in the studio almost until the end. He publicly confirmed his illness only one day before dying at his Kensington home from AIDS-related bronchial pneumonia at age 45.

John Lennon was an English musician, songwriter, artist and peace activist, best known as a founder, co-lead vocalist and rhythm guitarist of the Beatles and as one half of the Lennon–McCartney songwriting partnership. He died in New York City on 8 December 1980 after being shot outside the Dakota apartment building, shortly after returning from a recording session.

Simón Bolívar

Death date: December 16, 1830

Age: 47

Simón Bolívar was a Venezuelan military and political leader known as El Libertador for his central role in the independence of Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Peru, and Venezuela from Spanish rule. A visionary but often controversial statesman, he tried to unite parts of South America under Gran Colombia and became a lasting symbol of Latin American independence. In his final months, exhausted, politically isolated, and ill, he withdrew toward the Caribbean coast and died near Santa Marta on 17 December 1830, officially reported as tuberculosis, at the age of 47.

Birth date: December 18, 1906

Death date: November 9, 1982

Age: 75
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Leonid Brezhnev is highly controversial as the long-serving leader of an authoritarian Soviet state. His era is associated with political repression, censorship, dissident persecution, military intervention in Czechoslovakia, the invasion of Afghanistan, expanded security-state power, and economic stagnation.

Leonid Ilyich Brezhnev was a Soviet politician who led the Soviet Union from 1964 until 1982 as General Secretary of the Communist Party, shaping an era associated with Cold War power politics, détente, military expansion, and later economic stagnation. He had also served as head of state through the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet. In his final years his health visibly declined, and he died in Moscow on 10 November 1982, reportedly of a heart attack, ending one of the longest Soviet leadership tenures after Stalin.

Wilhelm II

Birth date: January 26, 1859

Death date: June 3, 1941

Age: 82
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Wilhelm II is controversial because of his association with German militarism, imperial expansion, aggressive diplomacy, and the crisis politics that preceded the First World War. Historians debate how much personal responsibility he bears for the war, but his reign is strongly tied to nationalism, authoritarian monarchy, and destabilizing foreign policy.

Wilhelm II, born Friedrich Wilhelm Viktor Albert, was the last German Emperor and King of Prussia, ruling from 1888 until his abdication in 1918 at the end of World War I. A grandson of Queen Victoria, he became a symbol of imperial Germany’s militarism, naval expansion, and turbulent diplomacy before and during the war. After losing the throne, he lived in exile at Huis Doorn in the Netherlands. He died there on 4 June 1941, aged 82, reportedly from a pulmonary embolism, while the Netherlands was under German occupation.

John Tyler

Birth date: March 28, 1790

Death date: January 17, 1862

Age: 71
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: John Tyler is highly controversial because he was an enslaver, defended slavery and states' rights, supported the Confederacy after secession, and was elected to the Confederate House of Representatives before his death.

John Tyler was the 10th president of the United States and the first vice president to assume the presidency after a president’s death, setting an important constitutional precedent after William Henry Harrison died in 1841. A Virginia politician, planter, and defender of states’ rights, he was expelled from the Whig Party while in office and later supported the Confederacy. Tyler died in Richmond, Virginia, on January 18, 1862, at age 71, before he could take his seat in the Confederate House of Representatives; his death was most likely caused by a stroke, and Confederate leaders gave him a state funeral.

Death date: February 20, 1677

Baruch Spinoza, also known by his Latin name Benedictus de Spinoza, was a Portuguese-Dutch philosopher whose radical rationalism helped shape modern biblical criticism, Enlightenment thought, democratic political theory, and debates about God, nature, freedom, and the mind. Excommunicated from Amsterdam’s Portuguese-Jewish community in 1656, he lived independently as a thinker and lens grinder while writing works such as the Theological-Political Treatise and Ethics. He died in The Hague on 21 February 1677 at age 44, probably from a lung illness often linked to tuberculosis and possibly aggravated by glass dust from lens grinding.

John Steinbeck was an American novelist and short-story writer whose work gave enduring literary force to the struggles of workers, migrants, families, and outsiders in twentieth-century America. He died in New York City on December 20, 1968, aged 66, of heart disease and congestive heart failure, after years as a heavy smoker.

B. R. Ivan Sergeyevich Turgenev was a Russian novelist, poet, playwright, translator, and one of the major voices of 19th-century realism. His story cycle A Sportsman’s Sketches helped shape Russian literary realism, while Fathers and Sons gave the world one of literature’s defining portraits of generational conflict and nihilism. In his final years he lived mostly in France, suffering from a painful malignant tumor that spread to his spine. He died at Bougival, near Paris, on 3 September 1883, aged 64, and was later buried in Saint Petersburg.

Zheng He was a towering Ming dynasty admiral, diplomat, explorer, and court eunuch who led seven vast treasure voyages across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433. Born Ma He in Yunnan to a Muslim family, he rose through imperial service and helped project Chinese power and trade from Southeast Asia to India, Arabia, and East Africa. He most likely died in April 1433 at Calicut, or during the final return from his seventh voyage; later tradition treats his Nanjing tomb as a cenotaph, suggesting his body may not have been returned.

Werner Karl Heisenberg was a German theoretical physicist and one of the central creators of quantum mechanics. He formulated matrix mechanics and the uncertainty principle, work that reshaped modern physics and earned him the 1932 Nobel Prize in Physics. During and after the Second World War he remained a prominent, sometimes controversial scientific figure in Germany. He died at his home in Munich on 1 February 1976 from kidney cancer, aged 74, and was later buried in Munich’s Waldfriedhof.

Aldous Huxley

Birth date: July 25, 1894

Death date: November 21, 1963

Age: 69

Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer, essayist, and philosopher whose sharp intelligence and restless curiosity produced nearly fifty books. He is best remembered for the dystopian classic Brave New World, as well as The Doors of Perception and influential essays on science, mysticism, society, and human potential. Born into the distinguished Huxley family, he became one of the most distinctive literary voices of the twentieth century. In his final years he suffered from cancer, which left him seriously weakened and, near the end, unable to speak. He died in Los Angeles on 22 November 1963, aged 69, on the same day as John F. Kennedy and C. S. Lewis.

Death date: December 20, 1375
