Giovanni Boccaccio was a fourteenth-century Italian writer, poet, scholar, and early Renaissance humanist, best remembered for The Decameron, one of the great works of European prose fiction. A friend and correspondent of Petrarch, he helped raise literature in the Italian vernacular to lasting cultural prestige. His final years were marked by poverty, illness, and declining health, including conditions later described as severe edema or dropsy. He died in Certaldo on 21 December 1375, aged 62.

Death date: January 27, 661

Age: 61

Ali ibn Abi Talib was a central figure in early Islam: cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad, husband of Fatima, fourth Rashidun caliph, and the first Imam in Shia tradition. Revered for his piety, legal judgment, eloquence, and courage, he became caliph in 656 during a period of deep political conflict after the murder of Uthman. His rule was marked by civil war and disputes over legitimate leadership. In January 661, he was struck with a poison-coated sword by the Kharijite Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam while at or entering the mosque in Kufa, and died from the wound shortly afterward.

Death date: December 12, 1784

Age: 75

Samuel Johnson, often called Dr Johnson, was one of the commanding figures of 18th-century English letters: a poet, essayist, critic, biographer, editor, and lexicographer best remembered for his Dictionary of the English Language. Brilliant, combative, witty, and deeply moral, he shaped English literary culture for generations. In his final years he suffered serious illness, including a stroke and worsening physical decline; he died in London on 13 December 1784 at the age of 75 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.

Death date: July 5, 1962

Age: 64

William Cuthbert Faulkner was an American novelist and short-story writer whose dense, experimental fiction transformed modern literature. Closely associated with Mississippi and his fictional Yoknapatawpha County, he wrote landmark works including The Sound and the Fury, As I Lay Dying, Light in August, and Absalom, Absalom!, and received the 1949 Nobel Prize in Literature. In his final years his health was weakened by drinking and repeated horse-riding injuries. He died of a heart attack in Byhalia, Mississippi, on July 6, 1962, at the age of 64.

Bertolt Brecht

Birth date: February 9, 1898

Death date: August 13, 1956

Age: 58

Bertolt Brecht was a German playwright, poet, theatre director, and one of the defining figures of modern drama. He reshaped 20th-century theatre through epic theatre, the alienation effect, and works such as The Threepenny Opera, Mother Courage and Her Children, and The Life of Galileo. Exiled after the Nazi rise to power, he later settled in East Berlin and co-founded the Berliner Ensemble. Brecht died in East Berlin on 14 August 1956 at the age of 58, commonly reported as the result of a heart attack after years of serious heart problems.

Why this is controversial: Andrew Johnson is one of the most controversial U.S. presidents. He opposed many Reconstruction protections for formerly enslaved people, clashed with Congress over civil rights and readmission of former Confederate states, used openly racist rhetoric, and became the first U.S. president to be impeached.

Andrew Johnson was the 17th president of the United States, a Tennessee Democrat and former tailor who rose from poverty to national office. He became president after Abraham Lincoln’s assassination and led the country through the turbulent early years of Reconstruction, becoming the first U.S. president to be impeached. After returning to politics as a U.S. senator, he suffered strokes while visiting his daughter in Tennessee and died on July 31, 1875, at age 66.

After years of political pressure and declining health, he died of lung cancer at his dacha in Peredelkino on 30 May 1960, aged 70.

After a final humanitarian trip to Somalia, she was diagnosed with a rare appendix-related abdominal cancer and died in her sleep at home in Tolochenaz, Switzerland, aged 63.

Pope Paul VI, born Giovanni Battista Montini, led the Catholic Church from 1963 to 1978 and guided it through the closing of the Second Vatican Council and the difficult first years of post-conciliar reform. He died at Castel Gandolfo on 6 August 1978 after a brief illness and a major heart attack, aged 80.

Why this is controversial: Ferdinand Marcos is highly controversial because his rule in the Philippines was marked by martial law, authoritarian government, corruption, political repression, censorship, torture, disappearances, and other serious human-rights abuses. Ferdinand Emmanuel Edralin Marcos Sr. was a Filipino lawyer, military officer, and politician who served as the tenth president of the Philippines from 1965 until he was overthrown in 1986. His rule included the declaration of martial law in 1972 and became associated with authoritarianism, corruption, and major human-rights abuses, while also reshaping Philippine politics for decades. After the People Power Revolution forced him into exile in Hawaii, Marcos spent his final years in declining health and died in Honolulu on September 28, 1989, from severe heart, kidney, and lung complications.

Rutherford B. Widowed after Lucy Hayes’s death in 1889, he died there on January 17, 1893, from heart disease or complications of a heart attack, aged 70.

Frédéric Mistral was a French Provençal and Occitan poet, writer, and lexicographer, best known for championing the language and culture of Provence and for co-founding the Félibrige literary movement. Death date: July 30, 1944

Age: 44

Antoine de Saint-Exupéry was a French aviator, writer, poet and journalist whose flying career shaped some of the most memorable literature of the 20th century. He worked on pioneering airmail routes across Europe, Africa and South America, and his books, including Night Flight, Wind, Sand and Stars and The Little Prince, combined adventure, moral reflection and poetic clarity. During World War II he flew reconnaissance missions for France. On 31 July 1944, aged 44, his aircraft disappeared over the Mediterranean during a mission near Corsica and Marseille; wreckage was later found, but the exact cause of the crash remains uncertain.

Death date: November 10, 1855

Age: 42

Søren Aabye Kierkegaard was a Danish philosopher, theologian, poet, and religious writer whose probing works on faith, anxiety, choice, and individuality helped lay the foundations of existentialism. Writing both under his own name and under pseudonyms, he challenged abstract systems of thought and the complacency of official Christianity. In 1855, after an intense public attack on the Danish state church, he collapsed in Copenhagen and was taken to Frederiks Hospital. He remained there for over a month, refused communion from the official clergy, and died on 11 November 1855 at the age of 42.

Sun Yat-sen, also known as Sun Zhongshan and Sun Wen, was a Chinese revolutionary, physician, and political leader whose work helped bring down the Qing dynasty and establish the Republic of China. In his final months he was gravely ill in Beijing; doctors found advanced cancer involving the liver, and later reassessments have pointed to gallbladder cancer that had spread. Aristophanes was the sharpest surviving voice of ancient Greek Old Comedy, an Athenian playwright whose political satire, outrageous fantasy, and verbal brilliance shaped the history of comic drama. He died around 386 BCE, probably in Athens, after a long dramatic career; no reliable ancient account preserves the cause of death, and later tradition mainly notes that his son Araros staged works connected with his final years.

Kim Jong-il was the second supreme leader of North Korea, ruling from 1994 after the death of his father Kim Il-sung until 2011. His rule combined a vast personality cult, military-first politics, severe repression, economic hardship and the development of North Korea's nuclear program. Ivan Alekseyevich Bunin was a Russian poet, novelist, short-story writer, and memoirist, celebrated for the classical precision and lyrical richness of his prose. In 1933 he became the first Russian writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature, with works such as The Village, Dry Valley, The Life of Arseniev, Cursed Days, and Dark Avenues securing his place among the major figures of Russian literature. After the Russian Revolution, he lived in emigration, mainly in France. Bunin died in Paris on 8 November 1953, reportedly after years of declining health; heart failure, cardiac asthma, and pulmonary sclerosis are commonly cited in accounts of his final illness.

Paul Dirac

Birth date: August 7, 1902

Death date: October 19, 1984

Age: 82

Paul Adrien Maurice Dirac was a British theoretical physicist and one of the founders of quantum mechanics and quantum electrodynamics. His Dirac equation predicted antimatter and helped reshape 20th-century physics; in 1933 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Erwin Schrödinger. In later life he worked at Florida State University, and he died in Tallahassee, Florida, on 20 October 1984 at the age of 82, where he was buried.

Kahlil Gibran was a Lebanese-American writer, poet, visual artist, and major figure of modern Arabic and English-language literature, best remembered for The Prophet, a 1923 work whose aphoristic spiritual prose reached readers around the world. Born in Bsharri and later active in Boston, Paris, and New York, he blended romanticism, mysticism, symbolism, and immigrant experience into a distinctive literary voice. He died in New York City on April 10, 1931, at age 48; contemporary accounts report cirrhosis of the liver, with incipient tuberculosis also noted.

Rafael José Orozco Maestre was a Colombian vallenato singer and one of the defining popular voices of the genre. Born in Becerril, Cesar, he became famous as the lead singer and co-founder, with accordionist Israel Romero, of Binomio de Oro de América, a group beloved across Colombia, Mexico, and Venezuela. His warm, lyrical style made him a lasting icon of Colombian folk-pop music. Anna Akhmatova, born Anna Andreyevna Gorenko, was one of the defining Russian and Soviet poets of the twentieth century. Associated with Acmeism, she became famous for the clarity, restraint, and emotional force of her lyric poetry, and later for major works such as Requiem, shaped by Stalinist terror, censorship, and personal loss. After suffering a heart attack in late 1965, she was convalescing near Moscow and died of heart failure in Domodedovo on 5 March 1966, aged 76. She was buried at Komarovo.

Age: 75

Titus Livius, better known as Livy, was a Roman historian from Patavium, modern Padua, whose vast work Ab Urbe Condita told the story of Rome from legendary origins to his own age under Augustus. His writing shaped how later generations imagined early Rome, republican virtue, and imperial memory. Livy died in AD 17 at Patavium, apparently in old age; no dramatic illness, execution, or accident is recorded, so his death is best described as a quiet end to a long literary life.

Giordano Bruno, born Filippo Bruno, was an Italian Dominican friar, philosopher, poet, cosmological theorist, and bold advocate of an infinite universe filled with innumerable worlds. Franz Peter Schubert was an Austrian composer who helped bridge the late Classical and early Romantic eras. Schubert died in Vienna on 19 November 1828 at the age of 31; the official diagnosis was typhoid fever, though later writers have discussed other possible causes.

Pope Pius XII, born Eugenio Maria Giuseppe Giovanni Pacelli in Rome, led the Catholic Church from 1939 to 1958, spanning World War II, the early Cold War, and major theological developments such as the proclamation of the Assumption of Mary. Admired for his diplomatic discipline and criticized for the limits of his public response to Nazi crimes, he remains one of the most debated popes of the twentieth century. In his final days at Castel Gandolfo, he suffered strokes and severe decline; his death on 9 October 1958 was recorded as acute heart failure.

Franklin Pierce

Death date: October 7, 1869

Age: 64
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Franklin Pierce is controversial because his presidency supported policies that strengthened pro-slavery political power and worsened the sectional crisis before the U.S. Civil War. The Kansas-Nebraska Act, violence in Kansas, and his alignment with Southern slaveholding interests make his legacy especially disputed.

Franklin Pierce was the 14th president of the United States, serving from 1853 to 1857 after earlier careers as a New Hampshire lawyer, congressman, senator, and Mexican-American War officer. His presidency is remembered for the Kansas-Nebraska Act and the worsening sectional crisis before the Civil War. In later life he became increasingly isolated, struggled with alcohol, and died in Concord, New Hampshire, from cirrhosis at age 64.

Hannibal Barca was a Carthaginian general and statesman, famous for leading Carthage against Rome in the Second Punic War and for his daring crossing of the Alps with an army that included war elephants. After Carthage’s defeat, he remained a political and military opponent of Rome in exile. He died at Libyssa in Bithynia, most likely by taking poison when Roman pressure made capture seem imminent.

Averroes, or Ibn Rushd, was a 12th-century Andalusian philosopher, jurist, physician, and one of the most influential interpreters of Aristotle. Born in Córdoba, he served as a judge and court physician and wrote major works on philosophy, Islamic law, medicine, astronomy, and theology. Late in life he fell out of favor under the Almohads and spent a period in disgrace before being restored to court circles. He died in Marrakesh in 1198 at the age of 72; his remains were later associated with a return to Córdoba, symbolically linking his death to the city where his intellectual life began.

Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Pol Pot is one of the most controversial and infamous figures in modern history because he led the Khmer Rouge regime responsible for the Cambodian genocide. His rule involved forced evacuations, mass executions, starvation, forced labor, persecution, and the deaths of roughly a quarter of Cambodia’s population.

Pol Pot, born Saloth Sâr, was the Cambodian communist leader who headed the Khmer Rouge and ruled Democratic Kampuchea from 1975 to 1979. His regime forced mass evacuations, radical collectivization, repression, and executions, becoming central to the Cambodian genocide. After losing power, he remained with Khmer Rouge forces near the Thai border. He died on 1998-04-15 at age 72 while under house arrest; heart failure was reported, though suicide allegations circulated and no autopsy confirmed the cause.

Robert Louis Stevenson

Birth date: November 12, 1850

Death date: December 2, 1894

Age: 44

Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish novelist, poet, essayist and travel writer whose restless imagination produced Treasure Island, Kidnapped, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, and A Child's Garden of Verses. Born in Edinburgh and often weakened by chronic respiratory illness, he turned poor health and travel into literary energy, eventually settling in Samoa, where he became known as Tusitala, the teller of tales. On 3 December 1894, at his home in Vailima, he suddenly collapsed after speaking with his wife and died within hours, probably from a stroke or brain haemorrhage. He was buried on Mount Vaea overlooking the sea.

Walter Scott

Birth date: August 14, 1771

Death date: September 20, 1832

Age: 61

Sir Walter Scott was a Scottish novelist, poet, historian, and lawyer whose Waverley novels helped establish the historical novel as a major literary form. Works such as Ivanhoe, Waverley, Marmion, and The Lady of the Lake made him one of the most widely read writers of the nineteenth century. After years of intense work, debt, and declining health, he suffered strokes, returned from a failed restorative journey abroad, and died at his home, Abbotsford, on 21 September 1832 at the age of 61.

Judy Garland

Death date: June 21, 1969

Age: 47

Judy Garland, born Frances Ethel Gumm, was an American actress and singer whose emotional range, musicality, and screen presence made her one of classic Hollywood’s defining stars. She became internationally famous as Dorothy Gale in The Wizard of Oz and built a career across film, stage, recordings, and television, earning major honors including Grammy Awards, a Special Tony Award, and an Academy Juvenile Award. Garland died in London on June 22, 1969, at age 47, from an accidental barbiturate overdose after years of health problems and dependence on prescription medication.

Mikhail Bakunin

Birth date: May 29, 1814

Death date: June 30, 1876

Age: 62
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Mikhail Bakunin is controversial because he was a revolutionary anarchist who endorsed insurrectionary struggle and the destruction of state authority. His writings include intense anti-state and anti-religious rhetoric, and some of his texts and private writings contain antisemitic language and conspiracy-minded attacks on rivals.

Mikhail Alexandrovich Bakunin was a Russian revolutionary anarchist and political philosopher, one of the central figures of 19th-century anarchism and a fierce opponent of authoritarian socialism. He took part in European revolutionary movements, endured imprisonment and Siberian exile, escaped through Japan and America, and later shaped collectivist anarchist thought. In his final years his health deteriorated after a life of agitation, prison, and exile; he retired to Switzerland and died in Bern on 1 July 1876 at the age of 62.

Herbert Spencer

Birth date: April 26, 1820

Death date: December 7, 1903

Age: 83

Herbert Spencer was an English philosopher, sociologist, psychologist, biologist, and political thinker whose ambitious evolutionary worldview made him one of the most influential Victorian intellectuals. He coined the phrase "survival of the fittest" and tried to connect biology, psychology, society, and ethics through his Synthetic Philosophy. In his last years he continued to write, often by dictation, while suffering from poor health. He died in Brighton, Sussex, on 8 December 1903 at the age of 83, and his ashes were later interred at Highgate Cemetery in London.

Gustav Mahler was an Austro-Bohemian Romantic composer and one of the most influential conductors of his generation, remembered for symphonies and songs that helped bridge 19th-century Romanticism and early modernism. Born in Bohemia to a German-speaking Jewish family, he rose through major European opera posts and became director of the Vienna Court Opera before later working in New York. His final years were marked by heart trouble and serious infection; after a last conducting season in New York, he returned to Europe and died in Vienna on 18 May 1911 at age 50.

Death date: August 29, 1940

Age: 83

Sir Joseph John Thomson was a British physicist whose work transformed atomic science. In 1897 he showed that cathode rays were made of tiny negatively charged particles, later called electrons, and he received the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics for research on electrical conduction in gases. He spent most of his career at Cambridge, shaping the Cavendish Laboratory into a center of modern physics. Thomson died in Cambridge on 30 August 1940 at age 83; his ashes were interred in Westminster Abbey near Newton and Rutherford.

Justinian I

Birth date: May 10, 482

Death date: November 13, 565

Age: 83
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Justinian I is highly controversial because his reign involved autocratic rule, brutal suppression of unrest such as the Nika revolt, expensive wars of reconquest, and persecution of religious and philosophical opponents. His legal and architectural achievements are tied to an imperial system that used severe coercion.

Justinian I, also known as Justinian the Great, was the Eastern Roman emperor from 527 to 565 and one of the most influential rulers of late antiquity. He is remembered for the Corpus Juris Civilis, the reconquest of parts of the western Roman Empire, and major building projects such as Hagia Sophia. In his final years he became increasingly focused on religion and succession politics; he died in Constantinople on 14 November 565, apparently at night in the imperial palace, and was succeeded by his nephew Justin II.

James Abram Garfield was the 20th president of the United States, a former Union general, educator, lawyer, preacher, and long-serving congressman from Ohio. Garfield was shot by Charles J. Guiteau on July 2, 1881, only months into his presidency, and died on September 19, 1881, after infections related to the wound.

George Eliot, born Mary Ann Evans, was one of the defining novelists of Victorian England, admired for the realism, moral complexity, and psychological depth of works such as Adam Bede, The Mill on the Floss, Silas Marner, Middlemarch, and Daniel Deronda. After marrying John Walter Cross in 1880 and moving to Chelsea, London, she became ill with a throat infection, made worse by long-standing kidney disease, and died on 22 December 1880 at the age of 61.

Herman Melville was an American novelist, short-story writer, poet, and sailor whose sea experiences shaped works such as Typee, Omoo, Billy Budd, and especially Moby-Dick, now regarded as one of the great American novels. Melville died at his New York City home on September 28, 1891, aged 72, with contemporary and later accounts describing heart failure, cardiac dilation, or a heart attack as the cause.

Guy de Maupassant was a French writer and one of the great masters of the modern short story, admired for his sharp realism, economy of style, and unsentimental portraits of society. His final years were marked by severe mental and physical decline linked to syphilis; after a suicide attempt in 1892, he was placed in a private asylum in Paris, where he died on 6 July 1893 at the age of 42.

James K. Polk was the 11th president of the United States, serving from 1845 to 1849, and is remembered for his forceful expansionist agenda, including the annexation of Texas, the Oregon settlement, and major territorial gains after the Mexican-American War. A former Speaker of the House and governor of Tennessee, he kept his pledge to serve only one term. Soon after leaving office, he returned to Tennessee exhausted and died of cholera in Nashville on June 15, 1849, at the age of 53.

Death date: March 7, 1869

Age: 65

Hector Berlioz was a French Romantic composer, conductor, and critic whose bold orchestral imagination reshaped 19th-century music. He is best known for Symphonie fantastique, Harold in Italy, the Requiem, Roméo et Juliette, La Damnation de Faust, and the opera Les Troyens. A brilliant writer on instrumentation and a forceful critic, he won more recognition abroad than in much of Paris during his lifetime. His final years were shadowed by chronic illness, depression, the deaths of loved ones, and a serious fall after a trip to Nice; he weakened gradually and died at his Paris home on 1869-03-08, aged 65.

Rising from Paris street singing to international stages, she became one of France’s most celebrated popular artists. Al-Ghazali was a Persian Sunni Muslim scholar, jurist, theologian, philosopher, logician, and mystic whose writings reshaped Islamic thought. Known as Hujjat al-Islam, the “Proof of Islam,” he is especially associated with The Revival of the Religious Sciences and with bringing Sufi spirituality into closer conversation with orthodox theology and law. After a brilliant teaching career in Baghdad, a spiritual crisis led him to withdraw, travel, and write some of his most influential works. Near the end of his life he returned to teaching briefly, then settled again in Tus, where he died quietly in December 1111 after prayer and retirement from public life.

His final years were marked by illness, poverty, and wandering after the An Lushan Rebellion; in 770 he died in Hunan, probably on or near a riverboat, aged 58.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Sukarno is controversial because his rule shifted from anti-colonial leadership into Guided Democracy, with authoritarian centralization, suppression of opponents, political manipulation among rival factions, and economic instability. His legacy is also tied to the violent political crisis that preceded Suharto's rise.

Sukarno, also known as Soekarno, was the charismatic founding president of Indonesia and a central leader of the country’s struggle for independence from Dutch colonial rule. A gifted orator and nationalist organizer, he proclaimed Indonesian independence in 1945 and led the young republic through revolution, state-building, and the turbulent era of Guided Democracy. After losing power to Suharto in the late 1960s, Sukarno spent his final years under house arrest as his health declined. He died in Jakarta on 21 June 1970 from kidney failure and related complications, aged 69.

Johan Cruyff was a Dutch footballer and manager whose intelligence, balance, and daring made him the defining face of Total Football. A three-time Ballon d'Or winner, he starred for Ajax, Barcelona, and the Netherlands, then reshaped Barcelona as a coach with the Dream Team era. Cruyff died in Barcelona on 24 March 2016 at the age of 68 after a battle with lung cancer, surrounded by his family.

Erich Maria Remarque

Birth date: June 21, 1898

Death date: September 24, 1970

Age: 72

Erich Maria Remarque was a German novelist whose anti-war classic All Quiet on the Western Front became one of the defining literary works about World War I. Born Erich Paul Remark in Osnabrück, he drew on his wartime generation’s trauma to write fiction about soldiers, exile, political violence, and moral survival in 20th-century Europe. His books were banned and burned by the Nazis, and he later lived in Switzerland and the United States. He died in Locarno, Switzerland, on 25 September 1970, aged 72, after serious health problems; sources commonly report heart failure, while some biographies mention an aortic aneurysm.

He died in Zushi on 16 April 1972, apparently by gas inhalation; the death was widely reported as suicide, although some close associates considered accidental death possible.

Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier was a French mathematician and physicist whose work on heat conduction led to Fourier series, Fourier analysis, the Fourier transform, and Fourier's law. He died in Paris on 16 May 1830 at age 62, after declining health; some biographical accounts connect his final decline with a fall down stairs at home.

Joseph Conrad, born Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski, was a Polish-born British novelist and short-story writer whose seafaring life and mastery of English prose shaped classics such as Heart of Darkness, Lord Jim, Nostromo, and The Secret Agent. Celebrated for moral tension, psychological depth, and dark imperial settings, he became one of the major figures of modern fiction. He died aged 66 on 3 August 1924 at his home, Oswalds, in Bishopsbourne, Kent, probably from a heart attack, leaving his final novel Suspense unfinished.

Henry David Thoreau was an American naturalist, essayist, poet, philosopher, abolitionist, and leading figure of Transcendentalism. He is best remembered for Walden, his classic meditation on simple living in nature, and Civil Disobedience, a powerful argument against unjust government authority. In his final years his health declined from long-running tuberculosis, worsened after a cold and bronchitis; he died at his mother’s home in Concord, Massachusetts, on May 6, 1862, at age 44.

Emma Goldman

Birth date: June 26, 1869

Death date: May 13, 1940

Age: 70
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Emma Goldman is highly controversial because she was a prominent anarchist revolutionary who openly opposed state authority, capitalism, militarism, and many social conventions of her time. She was linked in public debate to political violence because of the broader anarchist movement and her association with Alexander Berkman, though she also wrote extensively on free speech, labor rights, feminism, and birth control.

Emma Goldman was a Russian-born anarchist revolutionary, writer, lecturer, and one of the most influential radical voices in North America and Europe in the early 20th century. She campaigned for free speech, labor rights, women’s autonomy, birth control, and anti-militarism, and her fiery public presence made her both admired and feared. After years of imprisonment, deportation, and exile, she spent her final period in Canada. In February 1940 she suffered a severe stroke that left her partly paralyzed and unable to speak; after a second stroke in May, she died in Toronto on May 14, 1940, aged 70.

Gregor Johann Mendel was an Austrian Augustinian friar, teacher, botanist, meteorologist and mathematician whose pea-plant experiments in Brno laid the foundation for modern genetics. His work on dominant and recessive traits was largely overlooked during his lifetime but later became central to biology. In his final years, administrative duties as abbot limited his scientific work, and after a serious illness in 1883 he died in Brno on 6 January 1884, aged 61, most often described as from chronic nephritis or kidney failure.

Haile Selassie I, born Tafari Makonnen, was Emperor of Ethiopia from 1930 to 1974 and one of the most recognizable African leaders of the 20th century. He promoted modernization, helped bring Ethiopia into the League of Nations and the United Nations, and became a central symbolic figure for the Rastafari movement. Deposed by the Derg military junta in 1974, he spent his final months under house arrest in Addis Ababa. He died on 27 August 1975 at age 83; official accounts first described natural causes, but later evidence indicated he was likely strangled on the orders of the military regime.

John Calvin was a French theologian, pastor, lawyer, and one of the central figures of the Protestant Reformation. Based in Geneva, he shaped the Reformed tradition through his Institutes of the Christian Religion, biblical commentaries, and teachings on divine sovereignty and predestination. In his final years his health declined severely, including lung trouble and other chronic illnesses. He preached his last sermon in February 1564, said farewell to Geneva’s ministers in April, and died in Geneva on 27 May 1564 at the age of 54. He was buried in an unmarked grave to avoid turning his tomb into a shrine.

Convicted of treason, he was beheaded on Tower Hill in 1535 at the age of 57.

Joseph Goebbels was a German Nazi politician, philologist, and one of Adolf Hitler’s closest associates, best known as the Reich Minister of Propaganda from 1933 to 1945. J. Robert Oppenheimer was an American theoretical physicist best known as the scientific director of the Los Alamos Laboratory during the Manhattan Project, where he helped lead the development of the first nuclear weapons. Brilliant, cultured, and controversial, he later became a symbol of the moral burden carried by scientists in the atomic age. After years in public life and academia, he was diagnosed with throat cancer in the mid-1960s, likely connected to heavy smoking, and died in his sleep at his Princeton home on February 18, 1967.

Why this is controversial: Nicholas II of Russia is highly controversial because his reign involved autocratic rule, repression of political opposition, failures during the Russo-Japanese War, the Bloody Sunday crisis, antisemitic violence within the empire, and catastrophic wartime leadership during World War I. His execution and later canonization also make his memory politically and religiously disputed.

Nicholas II, born Nikolai Alexandrovich Romanov, was the last Emperor of Russia, ruling from 1894 until his abdication during the upheaval of 1917. His reign saw industrial growth but also deep political unrest, the Russo-Japanese War, the 1905 Revolution, and the strains of World War I. After abdicating, he and his family were held by revolutionary authorities and were executed by Bolsheviks in Yekaterinburg on 17 July 1918, ending the Romanov dynasty’s rule.

Paul Gauguin was a French Post-Impressionist painter, sculptor, printmaker, ceramist, and writer whose bold color, simplified forms, and Synthetist style helped move modern art beyond Impressionism. After years as a sailor and stockbroker, he devoted himself to art and became especially associated with Brittany, Tahiti, and the Marquesas. He died suddenly in Atuona on Hiva Oa in 1903, weakened by illness and pain; some accounts mention heart failure, morphine use, or other health complications. He was 54.

Arthur Rimbaud

Death date: November 9, 1891

Age: 37

Arthur Rimbaud was a French poet whose fierce, visionary writing helped reshape modern poetry before he abandoned literature in his early twenties. Associated with Symbolism and remembered for works such as A Season in Hell and Illuminations, he became a restless traveler and trader after his literary career. In 1891, after a painful knee tumor, his leg was amputated in Marseille; cancer continued to advance, and he died there on 10 November 1891 at the age of 37.

Hazrat Abu Bakr

Birth date: October 28, 573

Death date: August 22, 634

Age: 60

Abu Bakr, born Abd Allah ibn Abi Quhafa, was one of Muhammad’s closest companions, his father-in-law, and the first caliph of the Rashidun Caliphate. Revered in Sunni tradition as al-Siddiq, “the Truthful,” he led the Muslim community through the difficult transition after Muhammad’s death and oversaw the Ridda Wars and early expansion beyond Arabia. He died in Medina on 23 August 634 after an illness marked by fever, having nominated Umar as his successor, and was buried beside Muhammad in the Prophet’s Mosque.

Pius X

Birth date: June 1, 1835

Death date: August 19, 1914

Age: 79

Pope Pius X, born Giuseppe Melchiorre Sarto, led the Catholic Church from 1903 to 1914 and became known for his opposition to theological modernism, his support for Thomist theology, liturgical reform, frequent Communion, and the codification of canon law. In his final year he suffered poor health, including heart trouble and bronchial illness; as Europe slid into World War I, his condition worsened, and he died in Rome on 20 August 1914 at the age of 79.

Sully Prudhomme

Birth date: March 15, 1839

Death date: September 5, 1907

Age: 68

Sully Prudhomme was a French poet and essayist associated with the Parnassian movement, admired for disciplined form, philosophical reflection, and a wish to bring science and poetry closer together. In 1901 he became the first recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature and used much of the prize money to support poetry. His health had declined for decades after the Franco-Prussian War, and in his final years he lived almost reclusively at Châtenay-Malabry, suffering attacks of paralysis; he died suddenly there in September 1907 and was buried at Père-Lachaise Cemetery in Paris.

Robert Koch

Birth date: December 10, 1843

Death date: May 26, 1910

Age: 66

Robert Koch was a German physician and microbiologist whose work helped build modern bacteriology. He identified the bacteria responsible for anthrax, tuberculosis, and cholera, developed influential laboratory methods, and received the 1905 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his tuberculosis research. In April 1910 he suffered a heart attack and never fully recovered; he died in Baden-Baden on 27 May 1910 at the age of 66.

Rainer Maria Rilke

Birth date: December 3, 1875

Death date: December 28, 1926

Age: 51

Rainer Maria Rilke was an Austrian poet and writer born in Prague, widely regarded as one of the most important German-language literary figures of the modern era. His major works include Duino Elegies, Sonnets to Orpheus, The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge, and Letters to a Young Poet. Restless and cosmopolitan, he lived and worked across Europe before spending his final years in Switzerland. He had been seriously ill for some time, and his condition was eventually diagnosed as leukemia. Rilke died at the Valmont sanatorium near Lake Geneva on 29 December 1926, aged 51.

Taras Shevchenko

Birth date: March 8, 1814

Death date: March 9, 1861

Age: 47

Taras Hryhorovych Shevchenko was a Ukrainian poet, writer, painter, ethnographer and national cultural figure whose poetry collection Kobzar became foundational for modern Ukrainian literature and identity. Born into serfdom, he rose through artistic talent, studied in Saint Petersburg, and later became associated with the Ukrainian national movement. His exile and years of harsh military punishment severely damaged his health. He died in Saint Petersburg on 1861-03-10, shortly after his 47th birthday, reportedly after worsening illness and breathing difficulties; his remains were later reburied in Kaniv, Ukraine, in keeping with his famous poetic wish.

Adam Mickiewicz

Birth date: December 23, 1798

Death date: November 25, 1855

Age: 56

Adam Bernard Mickiewicz was a defining Polish Romantic poet, dramatist, essayist, translator and political activist, honored as a national poet in Poland, Lithuania and Belarus. His works, especially Pan Tadeusz, Dziady, Konrad Wallenrod and Grażyna, helped shape nineteenth-century Slavic literature and patriotic imagination. In 1855, during the Crimean War, he traveled to Constantinople to help organize Polish and Jewish forces against Russia; after falling ill, he died there, probably of cholera, at the age of 56.

Salvador Allende

Birth date: June 25, 1908

Death date: September 10, 1973

Age: 65

Salvador Allende was a Chilean physician and socialist politician who became president of Chile in 1970, leading the Popular Unity government and pursuing a democratic road to socialism through nationalizations, social reforms, and expanded public programs. His presidency polarized Chile amid economic crisis, political conflict, and Cold War pressure. On 11 September 1973, during the military coup led by Augusto Pinochet, Allende remained inside La Moneda Palace as it was attacked. He died there by gunshot, with later forensic findings supporting suicide.

John Ruskin

Birth date: February 7, 1819

Death date: January 19, 1900

Age: 80

John Ruskin was one of the defining intellectual voices of Victorian Britain: a writer, art critic, artist, lecturer, social thinker, and philanthropist whose works such as Modern Painters, The Seven Lamps of Architecture, and The Stones of Venice reshaped debates about art, architecture, nature, labor, and morality. In later life he suffered periods of mental illness and withdrew increasingly to Brantwood, his Lake District home, where he died of influenza on 20 January 1900 at the age of 80.

Birth date: May 23, 1905

Death date: February 20, 1984

Age: 78

Mikhail Sholokhov was a Soviet Russian novelist best known for And Quiet Flows the Don, his sweeping portrayal of Don Cossack life through revolution, civil war, and collectivization. Awarded the 1965 Nobel Prize in Literature, he became one of the most prominent official literary voices of the Soviet era. In later life he wrote little and lived mostly in Vyoshenskaya, where he died on 21 February 1984 at age 78 from laryngeal cancer.

Claude Debussy

Birth date: August 21, 1862

Death date: March 24, 1918

Age: 55

Claude Debussy was a French composer whose daring harmonies, fluid forms, and atmospheric orchestral color helped reshape modern music. Often linked with musical Impressionism, a label he disliked, he wrote landmark works such as Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune, Pelléas et Mélisande, La mer, and Clair de lune. He died in Paris of colon cancer on 25 March 1918, aged 55, while the city was under German bombardment during World War I, which made a large public funeral impossible.

Douglas Adams

Birth date: March 10, 1952

Death date: May 10, 2001

Age: 49

Douglas Noël Adams was an English author, humorist, screenwriter, and technology enthusiast, best remembered as the creator of The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy and the Dirk Gently novels. His comic imagination mixed science fiction, philosophy, absurdity, and sharp wordplay, making him one of Britain’s most distinctive modern comic writers. Adams died suddenly in Santa Barbara, California, after collapsing from a heart attack while resting from a workout at a gym; he was 49.

Edmund Burke

Birth date: January 11, 1729

Death date: July 8, 1797

Age: 68

Edmund Burke was an Anglo-Irish writer, philosopher, orator, and Whig politician, remembered as one of the most influential political thinkers of the eighteenth century and a major early voice of modern conservatism. He defended constitutional order, criticized the French Revolution in Reflections on the Revolution in France, and spoke powerfully on empire, America, India, and political responsibility. In his final years he suffered declining health, with sources describing serious stomach illness, and died at Beaconsfield, Buckinghamshire, on 9 July 1797 at the age of 68. He was buried there, in accordance with his wish for a private burial rather than a grand public memorial.

William James

Birth date: January 10, 1842

Death date: August 25, 1910

Age: 68

William James was an American philosopher and psychologist, a central figure in pragmatism, radical empiricism, and early functional psychology. A Harvard professor and author of The Principles of Psychology and The Varieties of Religious Experience, he helped shape modern thinking about consciousness, belief, emotion, and experience. In his final years he suffered from worsening heart trouble; after unsuccessful experimental treatment in Europe, he returned to New Hampshire and died of heart failure at his summer home in Chocorua on August 26, 1910.

Anwar Sadat

Birth date: December 24, 1918

Death date: October 5, 1981

Age: 62

Anwar Sadat was an Egyptian military officer and statesman who became the third president of Egypt, leading the country from 1970 to 1981. He reshaped Egypt after Nasser, launched the Infitah economic opening, led Egypt in the 1973 October War, and later made a historic peace with Israel, sharing the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize with Menachem Begin. Sadat died on 6 October 1981, aged 62, when members of Egyptian Islamic Jihad assassinated him during a military parade in Cairo.

Swami Vivekananda

Birth date: January 11, 1863

Death date: July 3, 1902

Age: 39

Swami Vivekananda, born Narendranath Datta, was an Indian Hindu monk, philosopher, author, and the leading disciple of Ramakrishna. He became one of the most influential modern interpreters of Vedanta and Yoga, gaining international fame after his 1893 address at the World’s Parliament of Religions in Chicago. He founded the Ramakrishna Mission and helped shape modern Hindu thought and Indian nationalism. After years of intense travel, teaching, and declining health, he died quietly at Belur Math on 4 July 1902, reportedly while meditating; a cerebral blood vessel rupture has been suggested as a possible cause.

Death date: September 27, 1978

Age: 65

Pope John Paul I, born Albino Luciani, was the Italian head of the Catholic Church and sovereign of Vatican City for just 33 days in 1978. Known as “the Smiling Pope,” he had served as Bishop of Vittorio Veneto, Patriarch of Venice, and cardinal before his election. His sudden death in the Apostolic Palace on 28 September 1978, apparently from a heart attack, ended one of the shortest pontificates in papal history.

Death date: January 9, 1957

Age: 67

Gabriela Mistral, born Lucila Godoy Alcayaga, was a Chilean poet, teacher, journalist, and diplomat whose lyric voice made her one of Latin America’s defining literary figures. In 1945 she became the first Latin American writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. Her final years were spent largely in New York, where poor health limited her travel; she died in Hempstead, Long Island, after pancreatic cancer, aged 67.

Neville Chamberlain

Birth date: March 17, 1869

Death date: November 8, 1940

Age: 71
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Neville Chamberlain is controversial because his appeasement policy toward Nazi Germany, especially the Munich Agreement, is widely associated with failed attempts to prevent war and with underestimating Hitler's expansionist aims.

Arthur Neville Chamberlain was a British Conservative politician and Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1937 to 1940, remembered above all for the Munich Agreement and the policy of appeasement toward Nazi Germany before the Second World War. After resigning as prime minister in May 1940, he remained in Winston Churchill’s wartime government for several months, but worsening illness forced him to step down. He died of bowel cancer on 9 November 1940 at the age of 71.

Tiberius

Birth date: November 15, 42 BCE

Death date: March 15, 37

Age: 77
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Tiberius is highly controversial as a Roman emperor associated in ancient sources with political repression, treason trials, executions, paranoia, and abusive rule, especially in the later part of his reign. Some modern historians question hostile ancient accounts, but his public image remains dark and disputed.

Tiberius Julius Caesar Augustus was the second Roman emperor, ruling from AD 14 to 37 after succeeding his stepfather Augustus. A capable soldier and administrator, he helped stabilize the early Roman Empire, though his later reign became associated with suspicion, political trials, and withdrawal from Rome. He died on 16 March AD 37, probably at Misenum after illness; ancient accounts differ, with some describing a natural death and others reporting rumors that he was smothered as Caligula’s succession began.

Death date: February 4, 2023

Age: 79
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Pervez Musharraf is highly controversial because he seized power in a military coup, suspended constitutional rule, imposed emergency measures, clashed with courts and civilian institutions, and presided over major security crises, military operations, and human-rights disputes.

Pervez Musharraf was a Pakistani army general and politician who seized power in a 1999 coup and served as Pakistan’s president from 2001 to 2008. A key U.S. ally after 9/11, he remains a divisive figure remembered for military rule, economic reforms, confrontation with civilian institutions, and major security crises. He died in Dubai on 5 February 2023 at age 79 after a prolonged illness, reported as amyloidosis, while living in exile for medical treatment.

Death date: November 28, 2001

Age: 58

George Harrison was an English musician, songwriter, film producer, and spiritual seeker who became internationally famous as the lead guitarist of the Beatles. Known as “the quiet Beatle,” he helped broaden the group’s sound through Indian classical influences and later built a distinguished solo career with songs such as “My Sweet Lord” and “Give Me Love.” In his final years he was treated for throat cancer, lung cancer, and a brain tumour; he died in Los Angeles on 29 November 2001 from cancer, surrounded by close family and spiritual companions.

Stefan Zweig

Birth date: November 27, 1881

Death date: February 21, 1942

Age: 60

Stefan Zweig was an Austrian novelist, playwright, journalist, and biographer, celebrated in the 1920s and 1930s as one of the most widely read and translated writers in the world. His works ranged from psychological fiction such as Letter from an Unknown Woman and The Royal Game to vivid biographies of figures like Marie Antoinette and Mary Stuart. Born into a Jewish family in Vienna, he went into exile after the rise of Nazism, living in England, the United States, and finally Brazil. In Petrópolis, increasingly despairing over the destruction of European culture and the war, he died by suicide with his wife Lotte in February 1942.

Death date: August 24, 1822

William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer whose handmade telescopes helped transform observational astronomy. He discovered Uranus in 1781, identified infrared radiation, studied double stars and nebulae, and became one of the most celebrated astronomers of his age. He died at Observatory House in Slough, England, on 25 August 1822, after a long illness, at the age of 83.

Lu Xun, the pen name of Zhou Shuren, was one of the defining writers of modern Chinese literature, famous for sharp essays, literary criticism, and fiction such as “Diary of a Madman” and “The True Story of Ah Q.” A major voice of the New Culture and May Fourth eras, he used satire and moral urgency to challenge old social habits and political complacency. He died in Shanghai on 1936-10-19 after prolonged ill health, commonly described as tuberculosis, at the age of 55.

Percy Bysshe Shelley was one of the great English Romantic poets, remembered for works such as “Ozymandias,” “Ode to the West Wind,” “To a Skylark,” and Prometheus Unbound. Brilliant, radical, and often controversial, he challenged political, religious, and social conventions and became far more influential after his lifetime. In 1822, while living in Italy, he drowned when his small sailing boat was caught in stormy weather on a return voyage from Livorno to Lerici. He was 29.

John Wayne, born Marion Robert Morrison, was one of the defining American film stars of the 20th century, especially known for Westerns and war films that made his rugged screen persona iconic. Nicknamed “Duke,” he worked with major directors such as John Ford and became closely associated with Hollywood’s Golden Age. He died in Los Angeles on June 11, 1979, at age 72, after a long struggle with cancer, with stomach cancer cited as the immediate cause.

Malcolm X, born Malcolm Little and later known as el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz, was an influential African American minister, public speaker, and Black nationalist leader. He rose to prominence as a major voice of the Nation of Islam before breaking with the organization in 1964 and founding Muslim Mosque, Inc. and the Organization of Afro-American Unity. A forceful advocate for Black dignity, self-determination, and human rights, he remains one of the most important figures of the civil rights era. Alexei Navalny was a Russian opposition leader, lawyer and anti-corruption activist, widely known as one of Vladimir Putin’s most prominent domestic critics. He founded the Anti-Corruption Foundation and used investigations, social media and political campaigns to expose alleged corruption among Russian elites. After surviving a Novichok poisoning in 2020, he returned to Russia in 2021 and was imprisoned. Navalny died on 16 February 2024 at age 47 in an Arctic penal colony, with Russian prison authorities saying he fell ill after a walk; his supporters and many international leaders blamed the Russian state for his death.

Death date: February 7, 1921

Age: 78

Peter Kropotkin was a Russian aristocrat turned anarchist thinker, geographer, and writer, best known as a leading theorist of anarchist communism and for works such as The Conquest of Bread and Mutual Aid. After years of exile and political activity in Europe, he returned to Russia after the 1917 Revolution but opposed Bolshevik authoritarianism. He spent his final years in Dmitrov, near Moscow, and died there of pneumonia on 8 February 1921; his funeral became one of the last major public anarchist demonstrations in Soviet Russia.

Death date: April 18, 1906

Age: 46

Pierre Curie was a French physicist and chemist whose work on crystallography, magnetism, piezoelectricity, and radioactivity helped shape modern physics. With Marie Curie and Henri Becquerel, he shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics for research on radiation. He died at 46 in Paris after slipping in the rain and being struck by a horse-drawn cart, a sudden accident that cut short one of science’s most brilliant careers.

Robert Schumann was a German composer, pianist, and influential music critic of the early Romantic era, known for poetic piano works, songs, chamber music, symphonies, and his role in shaping Romantic musical thought through the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik. His marriage to pianist Clara Schumann became one of classical music’s most famous artistic partnerships. In his final years, Schumann’s mental and physical health declined severely; after a suicide attempt in 1854, he lived in a private sanatorium near Bonn and died there on 29 July 1856 at the age of 46.

Death date: March 30, 1855

Age: 38

Charlotte Brontë was an English novelist and poet, one of the celebrated Brontë siblings, and the author of Jane Eyre, published in 1847 under the pseudonym Currer Bell. Her work brought emotional intensity, social criticism, and psychological depth to Victorian fiction. She married Arthur Bell Nicholls in 1854 and died in Haworth on 31 March 1855, while pregnant, shortly before her 39th birthday. Her death certificate recorded phthisis, though later scholars have suggested complications of severe pregnancy sickness may also have played a role.

Gamal Abdel Nasser

Birth date: January 14, 1918

Death date: September 27, 1970

Age: 52

Gamal Abdel Nasser was an Egyptian military officer and revolutionary leader who became one of the defining political figures of the modern Arab world. After helping lead the 1952 revolution that ended Egypt’s monarchy, he served as president, championed Arab nationalism, nationalized the Suez Canal, promoted major modernization projects such as the Aswan High Dam, and briefly led the United Arab Republic with Syria. He died in Cairo on 28 September 1970, aged 52, after suffering a heart attack shortly after the close of an Arab League summit, prompting massive public mourning across Egypt and the Arab world.

Anatoliy Solovyanenko

Birth date: September 24, 1932

Death date: July 28, 1999

Age: 66

Anatoliy Borysovych Solovianenko was a celebrated Ukrainian operatic tenor, admired for the bright lyric-dramatic quality of his voice and for a career centered on the National Opera of Ukraine. Born in Donetsk into a mining family, he first trained as an engineer before becoming one of Ukraine’s best-known classical singers, performing internationally and earning major Soviet and Ukrainian honors. He died suddenly in Kozyn, Ukraine, on 29 July 1999, from a heart attack, cutting short the life of a performer still strongly associated with Ukraine’s operatic tradition.

Charles V

Birth date: February 23, 1500

Death date: September 20, 1558

Age: 58
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Charles V is controversial because his rule was tied to imperial warfare, religious repression, dynastic domination, and the expansion of Spanish colonial power in the Americas. His reign overlapped with conquest, forced conversion, persecution of religious dissenters, and systems of extraction that caused severe harm to subject populations.

Charles V was the Habsburg ruler whose crowns linked Spain, the Low Countries, Austria, parts of Italy, and the Holy Roman Empire, creating one of the most formidable dynastic powers of the sixteenth century. As Charles I of Spain, he also ruled during the expansion of Spain’s American empire. Worn down by war, religious conflict, and chronic gout, he abdicated much of his power and retired to the Monastery of Yuste in Spain, where he became seriously ill, likely with malaria, and died in the early hours of 21 September 1558 at age 58.

Birth date: April 25, 1798

Death date: August 12, 1863

Age: 65

Ferdinand Victor Eugène Delacroix was a leading French Romantic painter whose dramatic compositions, expressive brushwork, and bold use of color helped shape 19th-century art. Best known for works such as Liberty Leading the People and The Death of Sardanapalus, he influenced later Impressionist and Post-Impressionist painters. After years of fragile health, a severe throat illness worsened in 1863; he died in Paris on 13 August 1863, aged 65, with his devoted housekeeper Jenny Le Guillou by his side.

Antoine Lavoisier

Birth date: August 25, 1743

Death date: May 7, 1794

Age: 50

Antoine-Laurent de Lavoisier was a French chemist, nobleman, and public administrator whose careful quantitative experiments helped transform chemistry into a modern science. He clarified the role of oxygen in combustion, helped reform chemical nomenclature, and influenced the development of the metric system. During the French Revolution, his former role in the tax-collecting Ferme générale made him politically vulnerable; he was convicted with other tax farmers and guillotined in Paris on 8 May 1794, aged 50.

Nero

Birth date: December 14, 37

Death date: June 8, 68

Age: 30
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Nero is one of the most notorious Roman emperors. His reputation is tied to political executions, alleged cruelty, persecution of Christians, violence within his own family, and the disputed but enduring association with the Great Fire of Rome. Some ancient accounts are hostile and partly propagandistic, but his public image remains strongly associated with tyranny and brutality.

Nero was the fifth Roman emperor and the last ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, reigning from AD 54 to 68. Remembered for his theatrical tastes, ambitious building projects, political violence, and the controversies surrounding the Great Fire of Rome, he remains one of antiquity’s most notorious rulers. Facing rebellion, abandonment by key supporters, and condemnation by the Senate, Nero fled Rome and died by suicide on 9 June AD 68 at the age of 30.

Marie Antoinette was an Austrian archduchess who became Queen of France as the wife of Louis XVI. After the monarchy was overthrown, she was imprisoned, tried by the Revolutionary Tribunal, convicted of high treason, and executed by guillotine in Paris on 16 October 1793.

Ada Lovelace was an English mathematician and writer best known for her visionary work with Charles Babbage on the Analytical Engine. Her notes on the machine included what is often described as the first published computer program, and she also understood that such machines could manipulate symbols beyond numbers. She died in Marylebone, London, on 27 November 1852, after months of illness from cancer, and was buried beside her father, Lord Byron.

Age: 36
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Maximilien Robespierre is highly controversial because he is closely associated with the Reign of Terror during the French Revolution, political repression, revolutionary tribunals, and mass executions by guillotine. His defenders point to his democratic, anti-slavery, and egalitarian positions, but his name remains strongly linked to state violence and ideological extremism.

Maximilien Robespierre was a French lawyer, Jacobin politician, and one of the most influential figures of the French Revolution. He championed political equality, universal male suffrage, civic virtue, and the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade, while becoming closely associated with the Committee of Public Safety and the Reign of Terror. In July 1794, amid rising fear of his power and policies, he was overthrown in the Thermidorian Reaction, arrested, and guillotined in Paris without trial at the age of 36.

Franz Beckenbauer was one of football’s defining figures: a graceful German defender and libero, captain of West Germany’s 1974 World Cup-winning team, and manager of the national side when it won the 1990 World Cup. Oliver Cromwell

Birth date: May 4, 1599

Death date: September 12, 1658

Age: 59
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Oliver Cromwell is highly controversial because he helped overthrow and execute Charles I, ruled through military-backed authority, and led brutal campaigns in Ireland, especially at Drogheda and Wexford. His legacy is sharply divided between reformer, revolutionary, dictator, and perpetrator of severe wartime atrocities.

Oliver Cromwell was an English soldier, parliamentarian and statesman who rose from provincial gentry to become one of the central figures of the English Civil Wars. A gifted cavalry commander for Parliament, he helped defeat the royalists, supported the trial and execution of Charles I, and later ruled England, Scotland and Ireland as Lord Protector. His legacy remains fiercely debated, admired by some for religious and political reform and condemned by others for military rule and brutal campaigns, especially in Ireland. He died at Whitehall in 1658, aged 59, probably after a severe illness involving malarial fever, urinary or kidney trouble, and likely sepsis.

Heinrich Theodor Böll was one of the defining German writers of the postwar era, known for morally sharp novels and stories about war, guilt, Catholic life, social hypocrisy, and the fragile rebuilding of German society. Böll died on 16 July 1985 at the age of 67, shortly after leaving hospital; contemporary reports said the cause was not publicly disclosed, though he had been ill for some time.

Emily Jane Brontë was an English novelist and poet, best remembered for her only novel, Wuthering Heights, a fierce and atmospheric classic of English literature published under the pen name Ellis Bell. Her health declined rapidly in 1848, soon after the death of her brother Branwell; she refused medical help until it was too late and died of tuberculosis in Haworth at the age of 30.

Edgar Degas was a French painter, draftsman, printmaker, sculptor, and one of the key figures associated with Impressionism, though he preferred to think of himself as a realist. In his final years, worsening eyesight left him increasingly withdrawn and nearly blind; he died in Paris on 27 September 1917 at the age of 83 and was buried in Montmartre Cemetery.

Christiaan Huygens was a Dutch mathematician, physicist, astronomer, engineer, and inventor, remembered as one of the great figures of the Scientific Revolution. In his later years, Huygens suffered from recurring illness, loneliness, and melancholy. He died in The Hague on 8 July 1695, aged 66, and was buried in the Grote Kerk.

Dag Hammarskjöld was a Swedish economist, diplomat, and the second Secretary-General of the United Nations, serving from 1953 until 1961. He helped define the modern role of the UN chief through preventive diplomacy, peacekeeping, and a strong belief in an independent international civil service. His work during crises in the Middle East and Congo made him one of the most respected diplomats of the twentieth century. He died at age 56 when his aircraft crashed near Ndola, Northern Rhodesia, while he was traveling to negotiate a ceasefire during the Congo Crisis; the exact circumstances of the crash have remained the subject of later inquiries.

In January 41 he was assassinated at the Palatine Games in a conspiracy led by Praetorian officers, ending his reign at age 28.

Luciano Pavarotti

Birth date: October 11, 1935

Death date: September 5, 2007

Age: 71

Luciano Pavarotti was an Italian operatic tenor from Modena whose radiant voice, charismatic stage presence, and crossover success made him one of the most famous classical singers of the modern era. Celebrated for roles in bel canto and Puccini operas, he also reached huge global audiences through recordings, television, charity concerts, and the Three Tenors. In 2006, during a farewell tour, he was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. After surgery and treatment, he died at his home in Modena on 6 September 2007, aged 71.

Nicolae Ceaușescu

Birth date: February 7, 1918

Death date: December 24, 1989

Age: 71
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Nicolae Ceaușescu is extremely controversial because he ruled Romania as a dictator, built a repressive police state, promoted a personality cult, censored dissent, imposed severe economic hardship, and was overthrown during a violent revolution.

Nicolae Ceaușescu was Romania’s communist leader from 1965 to 1989, serving as general secretary of the Romanian Communist Party and later as president. His rule combined nationalist independence from Moscow with an increasingly repressive police state, personality cult, censorship, and severe economic hardship. During the Romanian Revolution of December 1989, he and his wife Elena fled Bucharest, were captured, convicted in a rushed military trial, and executed by firing squad on Christmas Day.

John von Neumann

Birth date: December 27, 1903

Death date: February 7, 1957

Age: 53

John von Neumann was a Hungarian-American mathematician, physicist, computer scientist, and polymath whose work reshaped quantum mechanics, game theory, economics, functional analysis, nuclear strategy, and the architecture of modern computing. A brilliant and unusually versatile thinker, he worked at Princeton, the Institute for Advanced Study, Los Alamos, and the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission. In his final years he developed cancer, possibly linked by some accounts to wartime radiation exposure, and died at Walter Reed Army Medical Center in Washington, D.C., on February 8, 1957, at the age of 53.

Mohamed Morsi

Birth date: August 7, 1951

Death date: June 16, 2019

Age: 67
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Mohamed Morsi is a highly controversial political figure. He was Egypt's first democratically elected president, but his administration was accused by opponents of authoritarian tendencies, sectarian politics, economic mismanagement, and concentrating power through a disputed constitutional declaration. His removal by the military and later death in custody are themselves deeply contested parts of Egypt's modern political history.

Mohamed Morsi was an Egyptian engineer, academic, and politician who became Egypt’s first democratically elected president after the 2011 revolution. Affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood and its Freedom and Justice Party, he served from 2012 until he was removed by the military in 2013 amid mass protests. He spent his final years in custody facing several trials, and on 17 June 2019 he collapsed during a court session in Cairo and died soon afterward, with official reports citing a sudden medical episode while critics pointed to prison conditions and medical neglect.

George VI

Birth date: December 13, 1895

Death date: February 5, 1952

Age: 56

George VI, born Albert Frederick Arthur George, was King of the United Kingdom and the Dominions from 1936 to 1952. A reserved but dutiful monarch, he unexpectedly took the throne after the abdication of his brother Edward VIII and became a symbol of steadiness during the Second World War. He supported Britain through the Blitz, helped restore confidence in the monarchy, and was the father of Queen Elizabeth II. His later years were marked by serious smoking-related illness, including lung surgery; he died in his sleep at Sandringham on 6 February 1952, aged 56.

Birth date: December 31, 1863

Death date: September 1, 1937

Age: 74

Pierre de Coubertin was a French educator, historian, aristocrat, and the driving force behind the revival of the modern Olympic Games. He co-founded the International Olympic Committee and served as its president from 1896 to 1925, shaping Olympism as an international cultural and educational movement. He died suddenly of a heart attack in Geneva on 2 September 1937, reportedly in a park; he was buried in Lausanne, while his heart was later placed at Olympia in accordance with his wishes.

Solon of Athens was an archaic Greek statesman, lawmaker, poet, and one of the Seven Sages of Greece. Remembered for debt relief, legal reform, and weakening aristocratic domination, he helped prepare the ground for later Athenian democracy. He died around 560 BCE, probably at about age 70, with later traditions placing his death in Cyprus and linking his memory to Salamis; no reliable ancient source preserves a precise medical cause of death.

Amelia Earhart

Birth date: July 23, 1897

Death date: July 1, 1937

Age: 39

Amelia Earhart was an American aviation pioneer, author, and one of the most admired figures in early flight. She became the first woman to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic and used her fame to promote aviation, commercial air travel, and opportunities for women pilots. In 1937, while attempting to circumnavigate the globe with navigator Fred Noonan, she disappeared over the central Pacific near Howland Island. Despite major searches, neither she nor her aircraft was found, and her final flight became one of aviation history’s enduring mysteries.

Tycho Brahe

Birth date: December 13, 1546

Death date: October 23, 1601

Age: 54

Tycho Brahe was a Danish nobleman, astronomer, astrologer, and alchemist whose exceptionally precise pre-telescopic observations helped transform astronomy into a quantitative science. On the island of Hven he built Uraniborg and Stjerneborg, observatories that became centers of research, and his data later helped Johannes Kepler formulate the laws of planetary motion. He died in Prague on 24 October 1601, aged 54, after an acute bladder or kidney illness that followed a banquet; later studies found no convincing evidence that mercury poisoning killed him.

Age: 49
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Mehmed II is controversial as an imperial conqueror whose reign involved major wars, sieges, the fall and sack of Constantinople, population displacement, enslavement after conquest, and dynastic violence. He is admired in some traditions and remembered painfully in others, especially in contexts shaped by Ottoman expansion.

Mehmed II, known as Mehmed the Conqueror, was the Ottoman sultan whose capture of Constantinople in 1453 ended the Byzantine Empire and transformed the city into the empire’s great capital. A brilliant and ambitious ruler, he expanded Ottoman power across Anatolia and the Balkans while strengthening law, administration, architecture, and learning. In 1481, while setting out on another campaign, he became gravely ill near Gebze; gout was reported, and later accounts raised the possibility of poisoning. He died aged 49.

Francis Drake

Death date: January 27, 1596

Age: 56
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Highly controversial because he was a privateer involved in violent raids, imperial expansion, and early English slave-trading voyages. His reputation differs sharply between celebratory English naval history and perspectives that emphasize piracy, colonial violence, and slavery.

Sir Francis Drake was an English explorer, privateer, naval commander, and politician of the Elizabethan age, famed for completing the first English circumnavigation of the globe and for his role against the Spanish Armada. He was also involved in early English slaving voyages and became a feared raider of Spanish possessions. Drake died on 28 January 1596 during a failed expedition near Portobelo, Panama, most likely from dysentery, and was buried at sea in a lead-lined coffin.

Aretha Franklin was an American singer, songwriter, pianist, and cultural icon known as the Queen of Soul. Jean Racine

Birth date: December 20, 1639

Death date: April 20, 1699

Age: 59

Jean-Baptiste Racine was one of the defining playwrights of French classicism, admired for the concentrated power and psychological precision of tragedies such as Andromaque, Britannicus, Bérénice, Phèdre, Esther, and Athalie. A rival and successor to Corneille in the age of Louis XIV, he helped shape French literary taste through severe form, elegant alexandrine verse, and characters driven by passion, duty, jealousy, and guilt. He later served as royal historiographer and was a member of the Académie française. Racine died in Paris on 21 April 1699 at the age of 59, reportedly from liver cancer; he had wished to be buried at Port-Royal, and his remains were later transferred to Saint-Étienne-du-Mont.

Sigrid Undset was a Danish-born Norwegian novelist, best known for the medieval trilogy Kristin Lavransdatter and for receiving the 1928 Nobel Prize in Literature for her vivid depictions of Northern life in the Middle Ages. Robert Burns

Birth date: January 24, 1759

Death date: July 20, 1796

Age: 37

Robert Burns was Scotland’s national poet, a brilliant lyricist in Scots and English whose works include "Auld Lang Syne", "Tam o’ Shanter", "To a Mouse", and "A Man’s a Man for A’ That". Born in Alloway to a farming family, he turned everyday rural life, love, satire, and radical sympathy for ordinary people into poetry with lasting international appeal. He spent his final years in Dumfries as an excise officer while continuing to collect and reshape Scottish songs. His health declined sharply in 1796; modern experts often link his death to endocarditis, probably connected with earlier rheumatic fever. He died in Dumfries on 21 July 1796, aged 37.

Birth date: July 18, 1893

Death date: April 13, 1930

Age: 36

Vladimir Mayakovsky was a Russian and Soviet poet, playwright, artist, actor, and one of the defining voices of Russian Futurism. Famous for works such as A Cloud in Trousers and for his revolutionary public persona, he also created agitprop art and edited the avant-garde journal LEF. His relationship with Soviet cultural authorities became increasingly strained, especially after satirical works such as The Bedbug and The Bathhouse drew criticism. He died in Moscow on 14 April 1930 from a self-inflicted gunshot wound, leaving behind a career that remained politically celebrated yet personally turbulent.

F. Scott Fitzgerald was an American novelist, essayist, and short story writer whose work helped define the Jazz Age, a term he helped popularize. He is best remembered for The Great Gatsby, as well as This Side of Paradise, The Beautiful and Damned, and Tender Is the Night. His sharp portraits of ambition, wealth, romance, and disillusion made him one of the major American writers of the 20th century. G. K. Chesterton was an English writer, critic, journalist, poet, and Christian apologist, celebrated for his wit, paradoxes, essays, detective fiction, and the Father Brown stories. He died at his home in Beaconsfield, Buckinghamshire, on 14 June 1936, shortly after turning 62; contemporary accounts report congestive heart failure as the cause.

Birth date: February 2, 1809

Death date: November 3, 1847

Age: 38

Felix Mendelssohn was a German composer, pianist, organist, and conductor of the early Romantic era, admired for works such as A Midsummer Night’s Dream, the Italian and Scottish Symphonies, Elijah, the Violin Concerto, and Songs Without Words. A prodigy with a refined classical style, he also helped revive interest in J. S. Bach and founded the Leipzig Conservatory. In his final year he was weakened by overwork and devastated by the death of his sister Fanny. After a series of strokes, he died in Leipzig on 4 November 1847 at the age of 38.

Age: 55
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Henry VIII is highly controversial because of his authoritarian rule, executions of political and religious opponents, the deaths or executions of several people close to him including two wives, religious persecution, and the violent upheaval connected with the English Reformation and dissolution of the monasteries.

Henry VIII was King of England from 1509 to 1547 and one of the defining rulers of the Tudor dynasty. Famous for his six marriages, his break with Rome, and the establishment of royal supremacy over the Church of England, he reshaped English politics, religion, and monarchy. In his final years he suffered severe physical decline, including obesity and a chronic ulcerated leg wound, and died at Whitehall Palace in London on 28 January 1547 at the age of 55.

Did you know:

For most of history, a drink of water was also a gamble. Rivers, wells, and town pumps could carry sewage-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid. In the United States, typhoid fever was about 100 cases per 100,000 people in 1900; after water treatment, sanitation, and disinfection spread, it fell to 33.8 by 1920 and 0.1 by 2006. A glass of boring tap water may be one of the greatest inventions in history.

The humbling part is that this is not ancient history everywhere. WHO estimates that around 1 million people still die each year from diarrhoea linked to unsafe drinking water, sanitation, and hand hygiene. So when someone in a modern city turns a tap, showers, brushes teeth, and flushes a toilet without thinking, they are living inside a public-health miracle.
